title: Utility & fractional Kelly
text:
The framework gives a direct payoff for a belief: invest in the likelihood ratio \(L_M=\mathbb P^M/\mathbb P^Y\). That position maximizes expected log growth under the stated belief. It does not answer how much wealth an investor wants to expose to that belief, or which other preferences she might have.
Two familiar responses fit into the same language. Expected utility chooses a transformed payoff. Fractional Kelly allocates part of the budget to the original likelihood-ratio payoff and keeps the rest in the reference asset.
All wealth on this page is measured in units of the reference asset \(Y\). The formulas first describe a complete, finite-state market with positive pricing probabilities. Restricted asset menus require a further optimization over attainable portfolios.

title: Utility & fractional Kelly
text:
What utility maximization does
Let \(W\) be initial wealth and \(V(T)\) the terminal payoff. An investor with increasing, strictly concave utility \(U\) solves
\[
\max_{V(T)\geq0}\;\mathbb E^M[U(V(T))]
\]
subject to the pricing constraint
\[
\mathbb E^Y[V(T)]=W.
\]
Write \(p_i=\mathbb P^M(i)\) and \(q_i=\mathbb P^Y(i)\). An extra unit paid in state \(i\) contributes \(p_iU'(V(T,i))\) to expected utility and costs \(q_i\). At an interior optimum, the marginal utility per unit of cost is the same in every state with \(p_i>0\):
\[
U'(V^*(T,i))=\lambda\frac{q_i}{p_i}.
\]
If \(I=(U')^{-1}\) is inverse marginal utility, then
\[
V^*(T,i)=I\!\left(\lambda\frac{q_i}{p_i}\right).
\]
The budget fixes \(\lambda\). The resulting portfolio still induces a probability distribution,
\[
\mathbb P^U(i)=q_i\frac{V^*(T,i)}{W}.
\]
Utility therefore supplies a rule for turning the investor’s belief \(p\) and the market’s prices \(q\) into the implemented measure \(\mathbb P^U\).






NoteConditions behind the formula





The inverse-marginal-utility formula applies when \(U\) is continuously differentiable and strictly concave, with \(U'(0+)=\infty\) and \(U'(\infty)=0\). In the finite-state setting, a positive budget determines the multiplier uniquely. A state with \(p_i=0\) contributes nothing to the objective; paying it a positive amount would consume budget, so the optimizer assigns it zero. Utility at zero is interpreted through the boundary limit, and states of zero subjective probability do not enter the expectation.

title: Utility & fractional Kelly
section: Log optimality under the selected law
text:
Log optimality under the selected law
Let \(G^U=V^*(T)/W\) and suppose it is positive. The payoff selected by utility can be written
\[
G^U=\frac{d\mathbb P^U}{d\mathbb P^Y}.
\]
For any other positive unit-cost payoff \(G^V=d\mathbb P^V/d\mathbb P^Y\), the same identity used in the introduction gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E^U[\log G^U]-\mathbb E^U[\log G^V]\\
&\qquad=D(\mathbb P^U\Vert\mathbb P^V)\geq0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(G^U\) is log-optimal under its own induced law. Utility has selected that law from the original beliefs, prices, and risk preferences. For log utility, \(\mathbb P^U=\mathbb P^M\); other utilities generally select a different law. This observation does not require the investor to replace their forecast with \(\mathbb P^U\).

title: Utility & fractional Kelly
section: CRRA: a power of the likelihood ratio
text:
CRRA: a power of the likelihood ratio
Constant relative risk aversion uses
\[
U_\gamma(x)=\frac{x^{1-\gamma}-1}{1-\gamma},
\]
with \(U_1(x)=\log x\). Set \(\alpha=1/\gamma\) and \(L_M(i)=p_i/q_i\). The optimal gross payoff is
\[
G^U(i)=\frac{L_M(i)^\alpha}{\sum_jq_jL_M(j)^\alpha}.
\]
Its implied probabilities are
\[
\mathbb P^U(i)=q_iG^U(i).
\]
At \(\gamma=1\), \(G^U=L_M\) and \(\mathbb P^U=p\): utility reproduces the full Kelly position. For \(\gamma>1\), the power moderates the likelihood ratios. The denominator is essential: it makes the payoff cost exactly one unit of initial wealth.
For positive \(p_i\) in every state, increasing \(\gamma\) eventually brings the implemented measure back to \(q\). This is normalized geometric interpolation between the two distributions.
For the binary example \(q=(1/2,1/2)\), \(p=(2/3,1/3)\), and \(\gamma=2\),
\[
\mathbb P^U(\text{Win})=\frac{\sqrt2}{1+\sqrt2}
\approx0.5858.
\]
The induced Win probability lies between the market’s \(0.5\) and the investor’s \(2/3\). The construction is normalized geometric interpolation; the cash reserve below instead gives an arithmetic mixture.

title: Utility & fractional Kelly
text:
Fractional Kelly: keep a reserve
Invest a fraction \(f\in[0,1]\) of wealth in the full Kelly payoff and leave \(1-f\) in \(Y\). The gross terminal payoff is
\[
G^F(i)=(1-f)+fL_M(i).
\]
Multiplication by \(q_i\) gives
\[
v^F(i)=(1-f)q_i+fp_i.
\]
The original belief still determines the active position. The total portfolio’s measure is an arithmetic mixture because part of the budget stays in reserve. In particular,
\[
G^F(i)\geq1-f.
\]
This is a terminal wealth floor in units of \(Y\). With \(f=0.25\), at least three quarters of initial wealth remains even if the active position pays zero. It is not a claim about purchasing power in another unit, or about every strategy called “fractional Kelly.” Here the definition is a static holding of the reference asset and the full Kelly claim, without repeated rebalancing to a fixed risky weight.

title: Utility & fractional Kelly
text:
Compare the two portfolios
Start with \(\gamma=2\) and \(f=1/2\). Compare the state probabilities and the payoff floor. Keep the fraction linked to \(1/\gamma\) for a matched-parameter comparison, or unlink it to choose the reserve independently. Then increase risk aversion and try a belief that assigns zero probability to one state. The three-state view makes the difference between arithmetic and geometric interpolation visible.




Interactive comparison. It needs JavaScript.



Figure 1: The same market prices and subjective belief generate two moderated portfolios. Their expected log growth is evaluated under the original belief \(\mathbb P^M\); it is not the CRRA objective. The simplex shows the three probabilities as a single point.



The choice \(f=1/\gamma\) is a useful comparison, not a general equivalence. For beliefs close to prices, both gross payoffs have the same first-order expansion:
\[
G\approx1+\frac{L_M-1}{\gamma}.
\]
Further from the market distribution, their shapes and downside protection can differ substantially.






NoteWhy two states can conceal the difference



With two states and strictly positive beliefs, both families cover the segment from \(q\) to \(p\) for \(\gamma\geq1\), including cash as a limit. One allocation can be matched by a different parameter in the other family. They generally disagree at the same numerical \(\gamma\). With three or more states, they generally follow different curves, so changing one scalar parameter need not match the portfolios.








NoteWhat happens when a belief is zero?





For every finite \(\gamma\), CRRA retains the zero wherever \(p_i=0\). Fractional Kelly with \(f<1\) assigns that state positive mass through the reserve.
Let \(B=\{i:p_i>0\}\). As \(\gamma\to\infty\), the CRRA probabilities converge to
\[
\mathbb P^U(i)\longrightarrow
\frac{q_i\mathbf1_B(i)}{\sum_{j\in B}q_j}.
\]
Thus the cash limit requires full subjective support. Otherwise the limit is the pricing distribution conditioned on the states the investor considers possible.

title: Utility & fractional Kelly
text:
The information cost of moderation
Write \(D(P\Vert Q)\) for relative entropy and let \(v\) be either implemented distribution. The growth decomposition gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E^M[\log G]&=D(p\Vert q)\\
&\quad-D(p\Vert v).
\end{aligned}
\]
The difference from full Kelly is exactly the mismatch \(D(p\Vert v)\). That loss of expected log growth can be an intentional choice made for another objective or a wealth floor. It is measured under the stated belief; changing the belief can change the ranking.

title: Utility & fractional Kelly
section: When the asset menu is restricted
text:
When the asset menu is restricted
The formulas above solve the full-menu problem: each state’s payoff can be selected separately. With only a few traded assets, the chosen utility payoff may be unattainable.
Two distinct questions can then arise:

To maximize the original expected utility, solve \(\max_{G\in\mathcal A}\mathbb E^M[U(WG)]\) over the attainable, unit-cost payoffs \(\mathcal A\).
To approximate the full-menu target law, minimize \(D(\mathbb P^U\Vert\mathbb P^V)\) over the laws induced by \(G\in\mathcal A\). This maximizes \(\mathbb E^U[\log G]\).

These objectives need not select the same portfolio. They coincide for log utility under the original belief, and in special cases, but there is no general equivalence for other utilities. An already-selected positive constrained utility optimum is still log-optimal under its own induced law; that is a representation of the optimum, not a shortcut for finding it.
The portfolio-choice overview keeps the target, the available assets, and the optimization criterion separate.
Continue: explore mean–variance approximations, or choose among available assets in the portfolio laboratory.






NoteBook connection





Based on Chapter 3 of Jan Vecer’s Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective: “Utility Maximization” and “Risk aversion: utility-based density tempering versus fractional Kelly sizing.” The normal model shows how these constructions behave for Gaussian likelihoods.

title: Relative entropy
text:
Relative entropy answers a specific question: how much log evidence does one probability model expect to accumulate against another? In this information-theoretic view of finance, the same quantity measures an asset’s expected log return under its own implied measure.
The framework constructs an investment from probabilities. Here we slow down at the information-theoretic step: ratios, logarithms, and the probabilities used to average them.

title: Relative entropy
text:
First compare one observation
Consider two possible outcomes, A and B. The asset measure and the pricing measure assign these probabilities:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P^X&=(0.6,0.4),\\
\mathbb P^Y&=(0.5,0.5).
\end{aligned}
\]
If A occurs, its likelihood ratio is \(0.6/0.5=1.2\). That observation is 20% more likely under the asset model than under the pricing model. It favors \(\mathbb P^X\) over \(\mathbb P^Y\).
If B occurs, the ratio is \(0.4/0.5=0.8\). That observation favors \(\mathbb P^Y\). A likelihood ratio is a comparison between two specified models; it is not, by itself, a probability that either model is true.

title: Relative entropy
text:
Take logarithms so evidence adds
Independent likelihood ratios multiply. Taking their logarithms turns that multiplication into addition, which makes accumulated evidence easier to track. For our two outcomes,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log(1.2)&\approx+0.1823216,\\
\log(0.8)&\approx-0.2231436.
\end{aligned}
\]
Positive log evidence favors the numerator model; negative log evidence favors the denominator. Notice that the positive and negative values are not equal in magnitude. Multiplying wealth by \(1.2\) and then by \(0.8\) leaves \(0.96\) of the original wealth, so those two moves do not cancel.
We use natural logarithms throughout. Their information unit is the nat. A different logarithm base would rescale every information value; it would not change which model an observation favors.

title: Relative entropy
text:
Average using the first model
Now ask what the asset model expects. Under \(\mathbb P^X\), A has weight \(0.6\) and B has weight \(0.4\). Multiply each log ratio by that probability:
\[
\begin{aligned}
0.6\log(1.2)&\approx+0.109392934,\\
0.4\log(0.8)&\approx-0.089257421.
\end{aligned}
\]
Adding the contributions gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
D(\mathbb P^X\Vert\mathbb P^Y)\\
=0.6\log(1.2)+0.4\log(0.8)\\
\approx0.02013551\text{ nats}.
\end{gathered}
\]
The negative contribution remains part of the calculation. Relative entropy is an average of signed log evidence, not an average of absolute differences.
For any finite set of outcomes, write the two distributions as \(p=(p_i)\) and \(q=(q_i)\). The definition is
\[
D(p\Vert q)=\sum_i p_i\log\frac{p_i}{q_i}.
\]
Read the order carefully: divide first by second; average with first. This is also called Kullback–Leibler divergence, or KL divergence. We use \(D\) and \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) for the same quantity.

title: Relative entropy
text:
Try the calculation yourself
In the laboratory, A is called Success and B is called Failure. Move the asset probability first, then the market probability. Watch the individual log returns and their weighted contributions. Finally make the two probabilities equal: each ratio becomes one, every log ratio becomes zero, and relative entropy vanishes.

The interactive laboratory requires JavaScript. Its default example uses asset probabilities \((0.6,0.4)\) and market probabilities \((0.5,0.5)\). The corresponding returns are \((1.2,0.8)\) and the relative entropy is approximately \(0.02013551\) nats.

title: Relative entropy
text:
Why the average is nonnegative
The reason is the concavity of the logarithm: the log of an average is at least the average of the logs. This is Jensen’s inequality.
For the finite-state case, average \(q_i/p_i\) using the weights \(p_i\). Include only states with \(p_i>0\), so no division by zero is needed:
\[
\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\frac{q_i}{p_i}
=\sum_{i:p_i>0}q_i\le1.
\]
Applying Jensen gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
-D(p\Vert q)
&=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\log\frac{q_i}{p_i}\\
&\le\log\!\left(\sum_{i:p_i>0}q_i\right)\\
&\le0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(D(p\Vert q)\ge0\). Equality requires the ratio \(q_i/p_i\) to be constant on the support of \(p\) and all of \(q\)’s mass to lie there. Since both distributions sum to one, this means \(p=q\). If some \(p_i>0\) but \(q_i=0\), the divergence is infinite, so the inequality still holds.
Individual observations may support either model, but a model expects nonnegative log evidence in its own favor when the averaging uses its probabilities. This does not establish which model describes reality, nor guarantee positive evidence in a particular sample. Even in our example, a run of B outcomes can produce a large loss.
The order generally matters. Reversing our two distributions gives
\[
D(\mathbb P^Y\Vert\mathbb P^X)
\approx0.02041100\text{ nats}.
\]
The ratios are inverted and the averaging probabilities change. KL divergence is therefore asymmetric; it is not an ordinary geometric distance between two points.

title: Relative entropy
section: The financial meaning of the same calculation
text:
The financial meaning of the same calculation
Measure prices in units of a strictly positive traded reference investment, with distributions reinvested, so \(Y(T)=1\) in its own units. A nonnegative asset \(X\) with positive initial price and implied measure \(\mathbb P^X\) has gross return
\[
\frac{X(T)}{X(0)}
=\frac{\mathbb P^X(\omega)}{\mathbb P^Y(\omega)}.
\]
The likelihood ratios \(1.2\) and \(0.8\) are thus also the asset’s two wealth multipliers. Taking logarithms and averaging under \(\mathbb P^X\) gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E^X\!\left[\log\frac{X(T)}{X(0)}\right]\\
=D(\mathbb P^X\Vert\mathbb P^Y).
\end{gathered}
\]
The value \(0.02013551\) is an expected log return. It is not the expected ordinary percentage return. In this example, the expected gross return under \(\mathbb P^X\) is
\[
0.6(1.2)+0.4(0.8)=1.04,
\]
so the expected simple return is 4%. Averaging returns and averaging their logarithms answer different questions.
The superscript on \(\mathbb E^X\) matters just as much as the logarithm. An investor may hold beliefs \(\mathbb P^M\) different from the asset’s implied measure. If that investor assigns probabilities \((0.4,0.6)\) instead, the very same asset has expected log return approximately \(-0.06096\) under her beliefs. The nonnegative divergence identity becomes her expected-performance statement only when \(\mathbb P^M=\mathbb P^X\).

title: Relative entropy
text:
Continuous observations use densities
For a continuous observation, an exact point usually has probability zero under both models. Dividing those point probabilities would give no useful ratio. Instead compare densities with respect to the same underlying variable:
\[
\begin{gathered}
D(f_X\Vert f_Y)\\
=\int f_X(z)\log\frac{f_X(z)}{f_Y(z)}\,dz.
\end{gathered}
\]
This is the same instruction as before: take a density ratio, take its logarithm, and average under the first density. The normal model illustrates it explicitly with two bell-shaped curves and their likelihood-ratio price.

title: Relative entropy
section: From expected performance to long-run growth
text:
From expected performance to long-run growth
Why use expected log performance as a growth criterion? Repeat the same investment independently. Let \(p\) and \(q\) be the per-trial asset and market distributions, and write the gross return in period \(k\) as
\[
G(k)=\frac{p(\omega(k))}{q(\omega(k))}.
\]
Reinvesting the proceeds compounds these returns:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}&=\prod_{k=1}^{n}G(k),\\
\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}&=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\log G(k).
\end{aligned}
\]
The expected log return after \(n\) periods is \(nD(p\Vert q)\) under the asset model. More is true: if the observations are independent and identically distributed and the one-period log return is integrable, the strong law of large numbers gives
\[
\frac1n\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}
\longrightarrow D(p\Vert q)
\]
almost surely under \(\mathbb P^X\). This means convergence on a set of paths with probability one under the asset model. Relative entropy is the long-run log growth rate in this repeated experiment. The statement is conditional on the chosen model governing the observations; it does not establish that the model is correct.

The fair-game paradox
Under the market model, each return has mean one. Nevertheless, Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E^Y[\log G(1)]
&\le\log\mathbb E^Y[G(1)]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
For distinct positive \(p\) and \(q\), the inequality is strict. Averaging the same log ratios under \(q\) gives \(-D(q\Vert p)\). With the same independence and integrability assumptions, now under the market model,
\[
\frac1n\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}
\longrightarrow -D(q\Vert p)
\]
almost surely under \(\mathbb P^Y\). So typical market-model paths decay toward zero even though
\[
\mathbb E^Y[X(n)]=X(0)
\]
at every finite date. Increasingly rare, very large outcomes sustain the arithmetic average. There is no contradiction: average wealth across many possible outcomes and long-run growth along a typical path are different quantities. If \(p=q\), every multiplier is one and there is no growth or decay.
In our example the two long-run log rates are about \(+0.02014\) under the asset model and \(-0.02041\) under the market model. Generate paths in the binomial model to see the distinction. The linear information flow page develops the common additive structure across model families.






NoteMarket averaging, zeros, and support





When both distributions are positive, averaging the same log return under the market measure reverses the divergence:
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E^Y\!\left[\log\frac{X(T)}{X(0)}\right]\\
=-D(\mathbb P^Y\Vert\mathbb P^X).
\end{gathered}
\]
In the example this is approximately \(-0.02041100\), even though the market’s expected gross return is one.
Throughout the finite-state construction, market state prices satisfy \(q_i>0\). Asset probabilities may be zero: the convention \(0\log(0/q_i)=0\) reflects the limiting value of that expression. If \(p_i=0\) while \(q_i>0\), the asset pays zero in that state. Its expected log return under a model assigning positive probability to that state is \(-\infty\); the corresponding reverse divergence is \(+\infty\). In independent repetitions under the market model, such a state is eventually encountered with probability one, and reinvested wealth then stays at zero. The finite-log-mean assumption for the displayed market strong law does not apply in this case.
For general density models, positive mass under the numerator outside the denominator’s support gives infinite divergence. Finite subtraction identities require suitable support and integrability assumptions; one must not subtract two infinities.



Source: Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, Chapters 1–3. Continue to utility and risk aversion to see how an investor’s chosen payoff can differ from the belief-matching investment.

title: Portfolio laboratory
text:
A desired probability distribution need not be attainable with the assets a market offers. The trinomial model makes that restriction visible. This laboratory turns it into a portfolio problem: enter the distributions carried by the available assets, then find their best mixture for your belief.
This is a finite-state, one-period model. Every number describes the same scenario and horizon, and all prices and payoffs use the same reference asset \(Y\).

title: Portfolio laboratory
section: A portfolio is a mixture of measures
text:
A portfolio is a mixture of measures
Write \(q_i=\mathbb P^Y(i)>0\) for market pricing probabilities, \(p_i=\mathbb P^M(i)\) for beliefs, and \(a_{ji}=\mathbb P^{A_j}(i)\) for the distribution carried by asset \(j\). A unit of initial wealth invested in that asset pays
\[
G^j(i)=\frac{a_{ji}}{q_i}.
\]
Allocate cost weights \(w_j\geq0\) with \(\sum_jw_j=1\). The portfolio’s distribution is
\[
v_i=\sum_jw_ja_{ji},
\]
and its gross payoff is
\[
G(i)=\frac{v_i}{q_i}.
\]
The weights are fractions of the initial budget, not numbers of shares. If the initial asset price is \(A_j(0)\) and total wealth is \(W\), the holding is \(w_jW/A_j(0)\) units. A reference-asset holding has density \(a_{0i}=q_i\) and gross payoff one.

title: Portfolio laboratory
section: Enter a market and a belief
text:
Enter a market and a belief
Each row is a distribution across the same states. For example, “state 1” must mean the same outcome in the market row, belief row and every asset row. The table accepts 2–12 states and up to eight risky asset distributions; the reference asset is always available. Apply the inputs to normalize proportional weights explicitly. The market row must remain strictly positive; beliefs and asset rows may contain zeros.
Choose Columbia: Win claim + cash to reproduce the introductory football example. Select exact KL and click Find the best mixture: the optimal Win-claim cost weight is \(0.2\), the implemented law is \((0.6,0.24,0.16)\), and growth is \(0.0201355\) nats. The Draw/Loss ratio remains the market’s \(60{:}40\).
The default book example supplies a second incomplete three-state market. Solve for log growth and inspect the residual mismatch. Then try the four-state menu or the fully spanned state-claim preset. You can also change an asset density or add another asset. A larger menu can improve the best attainable growth, but it need not change the optimum if the added asset provides no useful new exposure.




Interactive portfolio laboratory. It needs JavaScript.



Figure 1: Editable pricing, belief and asset distributions. The solver chooses long-only cost weights. The displayed density and payoff describe the same portfolio; its expected log growth is always evaluated under the belief row, whichever optimization criterion is selected.









TipA useful three-step experiment




Solve with the default asset menu. Inspect where the implemented distribution misses the belief.
Add an asset whose distribution equals your belief. Under exact log optimization, the mismatch can now reach zero.
Change that asset so it no longer matches. Compare the exact log and quadratic solutions, then inspect their statewise payoffs.

title: Portfolio laboratory
text:
What the exact solver minimizes
Use \(D(P\Vert Q)\) for KL divergence. Expected log growth satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E^M[\log G]&=D(p\Vert q)\\
&\quad-D(p\Vert v).
\end{aligned}
\]
For fixed prices and beliefs, the first term is constant. The exact problem is therefore
\[
\min_{w\in\Delta}\;D\bigl(p\Vert v(w)\bigr),
\]
where \(\Delta\) is the simplex of nonnegative weights summing to one.
The feasible distributions form the convex hull of the asset rows. The optimizer finds the closest point in that set in the stated direction of KL divergence. Reversing the arguments would solve a different problem.
If \(p\) lies in the hull, the full likelihood-ratio payoff is attainable. If it lies outside, the minimum divergence is the exact amount of expected log growth lost because of the restricted menu. The portfolio measure may be unique even when several weight vectors implement it.






NoteWhy this optimization is convex





Ignoring a constant independent of \(w\), the objective is
\[
-\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\log v_i.
\]
Each \(v_i\) is linear in \(w\), and \(-\log\) is convex. The simplex of nonnegative weights summing to one is a convex feasible set. A valid first-order optimum is therefore globally optimal within this menu and these constraints.
For finite growth, every state with \(p_i>0\) needs \(v_i>0\). If all available assets assign zero mass to such a state, every allocation has expected log growth \(-\infty\). Including the reference asset guarantees a feasible portfolio with finite growth.

title: Portfolio laboratory
text:
Read the numerical result
The reported expected growth uses natural logarithms, so it is measured in nats over the chosen horizon. It is model-implied expected log return, not a promised return and not automatically an annual rate. The payoff table provides the statewise outcomes that produce it.
A numerical optimum is assessed by its first-order gap. For exact log growth, define the marginal improvement of asset \(j\) by
\[
b_j=\sum_{i:p_i>0}\frac{p_ia_{ji}}{v_i}.
\]
At a finite feasible portfolio, \(\sum_jw_jb_j=1\). The gap
\[
\delta=\max_jb_j-1
\]
bounds the remaining possible improvement in expected log growth. A small gap certifies that the current allocation is close to the global optimum in objective value. It does not guarantee that every individual weight is close to a unique target; redundant assets can give many equivalent portfolios.

title: Portfolio laboratory
section: Why the quadratic solution can differ
text:
Why the quadratic solution can differ
The laboratory offers exact log growth, the book’s mixed quadratic and classical mean–variance. The mean–variance page also explains their relation to the ordinary Taylor approximation. Exact log growth minimizes \(D(p\Vert v)\). The mixed quadratic minimizes
\[
\frac12\sum_i\frac{(v_i-p_i)^2}{q_i}.
\]
Classical mean–variance instead uses the portfolio mean and covariance under the subjective measure. It has a separate risk-penalty parameter. These are different objectives on the same feasible set; comparing their exact log growth afterward makes the consequences visible.
Long-only mixtures guarantee a nonnegative payoff and make the feasible set easy to interpret. Short selling would enlarge the set to affine combinations, with an additional statewise constraint to keep the payoff nonnegative. That extension changes the feasible geometry and is outside this laboratory.
Continue: options provide concrete asset-density shapes that can serve as portfolio ingredients. Utility and fractional Kelly explain how a preference or reserve rule changes the target portfolio.






NoteBook connection





Based on Chapter 1 of Jan Vecer’s Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, especially the theorem “State price density of a general static portfolio,” together with the constrained portfolio problems and information projections in Chapter 3. The finite-state laboratory illustrates these constructions without introducing a dynamic trading rule.

title: Options as distributions
text:
A call pays in high-price states. A put pays in low-price states. Their densities show which observations the contracts emphasize, including how much weight each observation receives. Here we draw those densities continuously, using the normal model.
Throughout, prices are in units of the reference asset \(Y\), so \(Y(t)=1\). The underlying is \(X(t)\), and a strike \(K\) is fixed in those units. We return to currency prices below.

title: Options as distributions
text:
Three densities on one axis
Let \(z\) be the standardized normal observation at maturity \(T\), and set \(a=\sigma\sqrt T\). The market and asset assign it different normal laws:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f^Y(z)&=\varphi(z),\\
f^X(z)&=\varphi(z-a),
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\varphi\) is the standard normal density. Thus \(z\) has mean zero under \(\mathbb P^Y\) and mean \(a\) under \(\mathbb P^X\), with variance one under both.
Dividing the densities determines the terminal price:
\[
\frac{X(T)}{X(0)}
=\frac{f^X(z)}{f^Y(z)}
=\exp\!\left(az-\frac{a^2}{2}\right).
\]
The observation is normal; the price is lognormal. This is the geometric Brownian motion model from the normal-model page, not a model in which the price itself is normally distributed.
Now choose an option payoff \(h(X(T))\). Its price and density are
\[
C(0)=\mathbb E^Y[h(X(T))],
\]
\[
f^C(z)=\frac{h(X(T))}{C(0)}\,f^Y(z).
\]
Multiply the market density by the payoff, then divide by its price. For a positive finite price, the result has area one. A call has no density below the exercise threshold; above it, larger payoffs receive more weight.

title: Options as distributions
text:
Draw the option’s view
Start with a call at strike 100. The blue and green curves are the two normal densities; the purple curve is the option’s induced density. Switch to a digital: its flat payoff above the strike conditions the market density on that region, without the call’s extra weighting toward larger gains.

The interactive density explorer requires JavaScript. With \(X(0)=K=100\), \(\sigma=0.25\) and \(T=1\), the call price is approximately \(9.948\). Its density is proportional to \(\bigl(100\varphi(z-0.25)-100\varphi(z)\bigr)^+\).

The density plot uses the normal observation \(z\) throughout. The separate payoff plot uses the terminal price \(X(T)\). Changing coordinates would change density heights; keeping a common observation axis makes the likelihood ratios directly visible.






NoteWhat this density means



\(\mathbb P^C\) describes the exposure built into one contract. It is not automatically the investor’s subjective forecast \(\mathbb P^M\). It also differs from recovering the underlying’s market distribution from a whole surface of option prices.

title: Options as distributions
section: A call price is a difference of two probabilities
text:
A call price is a difference of two probabilities
Let \(A=\{X(T)>K\}\). The call pays the underlying on \(A\), less the strike payment on the same event. Since \(X(T)f^Y=X(0)f^X\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
C(0)
&=X(0)\mathbb P^X(A)\\
&\quad-K\mathbb P^Y(A).
\end{aligned}
\]
The underlying payment is valued using the asset measure; the strike payment is valued using the reference measure. This identity holds before choosing any particular distribution.
Its density has an equally direct expression:
\[
f^C(z)
=\frac{\bigl(X(0)f^X(z)-Kf^Y(z)\bigr)^+}{C(0)}.
\]
The numerator is the positive part of the difference between two scaled densities. Its integral is the call price.

title: Options as distributions
text:
Black–Scholes from the normal tails
In the normal model, exercise means
\[
z>\frac{\log(K/X(0))}{a}+\frac a2.
\]
Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function, and define
\[
\begin{aligned}
d(2)&=\frac{\log(X(0)/K)}{a}-\frac a2,\\
d(1)&=d(2)+a.
\end{aligned}
\]
Under \(\mathbb P^Y\), the observation has mean zero; under \(\mathbb P^X\), its mean is shifted by \(a\). The exercise probabilities are therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P^Y(A)&=\Phi(d(2)),\\
\mathbb P^X(A)&=\Phi(d(1)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitute them into the two-measure price identity:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
C(0)&=X(0)\Phi(d(1))\\
&\quad-K\Phi(d(2)).
\end{aligned}}
\]
This is the Black–Scholes call formula in reference-asset units. The two normal probabilities have financial roles: one values delivery of the underlying, the other values payment of the strike. Neither probability is an investor’s personal forecast unless that investor chooses the corresponding measure.
For a put, use the complementary exercise region:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(0)&=K\Phi(-d(2))\\
&\quad-X(0)\Phi(-d(1)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Subtracting yields put–call parity,
\[
C(0)-P(0)=X(0)-K.
\]






NoteThe familiar currency formula, with interest





Let the reference asset be a bank account \(B(t)=e^{rt}\) with constant rate \(r\) and \(B(0)=1\). For a non-dividend-paying stock with currency price \(S(t)\), we have \(X(t)=S(t)/B(t)\). A currency strike \(K^{\mathrm{cash}}\) at maturity becomes \(K=K^{\mathrm{cash}}e^{-rT}\) in reference units.
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
C^{\mathrm{cash}}(0)
&=S(0)\Phi(d(1))\\
&\quad-K^{\mathrm{cash}}e^{-rT}\Phi(d(2)),
\end{aligned}
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
d(1)&=\frac{\log(S(0)/K^{\mathrm{cash}})+rT}{\sigma\sqrt T}\\
&\quad+\frac{\sigma\sqrt T}{2},\\
d(2)&=d(1)-\sigma\sqrt T.
\end{aligned}
\]
The discount factor appears when converting the currency strike into reference units. It was already accounted for by the choice of units above.

title: Options as distributions
section: Other payoffs, and a reference-asset reserve
text:
Other payoffs, and a reference-asset reserve
A digital call pays one unit on \(A\). Its price is \(\mathbb P^Y(A)=\Phi(d(2))\), and its induced distribution is \(\mathbb P^Y\) conditioned on \(A\).
A straddle combines a call and a put. Its density is the mixture of their densities with weights \(C(0)/(C(0)+P(0))\) and \(P(0)/(C(0)+P(0))\). The weights are fractions of the initial cost, even though the position holds one unit of each contract.
Calls, puts and digitals pay zero on entire regions. If an investor assigns positive probability to a zero-payoff region, committing all wealth to that option gives expected log performance \(-\infty\). The option density is still perfectly valid.
To retain a positive payoff floor, keep a fraction \(b\) of the budget in \(Y\) and allocate \(1-b\) to the option. The portfolio density is
\[
f^V(z)=b\,f^Y(z)+(1-b)f^C(z),
\]
and its gross payoff is at least \(b\). The explorer’s reserve control draws this mixture in gold. It is the same cost-weighted construction used in portfolio mixtures.
How could trading the underlying reproduce one of these payoffs? The discrete-hedging page compares a target density with the density implemented by rebalancing at finitely many dates.






NoteBook connection





Based on Chapter 4 of Jan Vecer’s Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective: “Option Payoffs,” the call and put induced distributions, the two-measure price identity, and “Black–Scholes Formula from State Prices.” The normal driver is the standardized cumulative return used there. Chapter 5 develops the same likelihood ratio as an additive normal model.

title: The negative-binomial model
text:
Start with the binomial example: the stock rises by \(u=3/2\) or falls by \(d=1/2\), with up probabilities \(1/2\) under the market law, \(3/4\) under the stock law, and \(2/3\) under investor beliefs.
One completed shock consists of \(G\) down moves followed by the first up move. For example, \(G=0\) means an immediate up move; \(G=2\) means down, down, up. The duration is \(\tau=G+1\) binary trials. This page changes the observation clock; the portfolio comparison also restricts trading to the boundaries between shocks.

title: The negative-binomial model
section: Three laws for the same geometric shock
text:
Three laws for the same geometric shock
Let \(a^Y=1/2\), \(a^X=1/4\), and \(a^M=1/3\) denote the down probabilities. For \(g=0,1,2,\ldots\),
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathbb P^i(G=g)=(1-a^i)(a^i)^g,\\
i\in\{Y,X,M\}.
\end{gathered}
\]
Consequently, the stock return and desired likelihood payoff are
\[
R=\frac{\mathbb P^X(G)}{\mathbb P^Y(G)}
=\frac32\left(\frac12\right)^G.
\]
\[
L_M=\frac{\mathbb P^M(G)}{\mathbb P^Y(G)}
=\frac43\left(\frac23\right)^G.
\]

title: The negative-binomial model
section: From geometric shocks to a negative-binomial count
text:
From geometric shocks to a negative-binomial count
Independent shocks \(G(1),\ldots,G(n)\) give the total number of down moves
\[
Z(n)=G(1)+\cdots+G(n).
\]
Under each law,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P^i(Z(n)=k)\\
&\quad=\binom{n+k-1}{k}(1-a^i)^n(a^i)^k,\\
&\qquad k=0,1,\ldots.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the negative-binomial convention used here: count down moves before the \(n\)th up move. Other texts may exchange the names “success” and “failure”; the displayed mass function fixes the convention without ambiguity.
The combinatorial factor cancels in the likelihood ratio:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}
&=\left(\frac{a^X}{a^Y}\right)^{Z(n)}
\left(\frac{1-a^X}{1-a^Y}\right)^n\\
&=u^n d^{Z(n)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the log price is affine in accumulated count and completed shocks:
\[
\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}=A Z(n)+Bn,
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\log\frac{a^X}{a^Y},\\
B&=\log\frac{1-a^X}{1-a^Y}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The one-shock likelihood ratio has expectation one under \(\mathbb P^Y\). Products across independent shocks therefore form a positive \(\mathbb P^Y\)-martingale; their reciprocals form a \(\mathbb P^X\)-martingale. This follows directly from the geometric laws, without requiring an unrestricted optional-stopping argument.

The interactive figure requires JavaScript. At the Columbia settings \(a^X=1/4\), \(a^Y=1/2\), and \(a^M=1/3\), ideal information is \(0.0849495\) nats per completed shock, while the stock’s own-law information is \(0.1744160\) nats per shock.

The first plot compares the market, stock, and investor laws on the same count axis. The price and log-price simulations show the same six paths under each of \(\mathbb P^X\) and \(\mathbb P^Y\), sampled at completed shocks. Trials inside each shock are not displayed. The infinite distributions are truncated only for plotting; neither their displayed probabilities nor the simulated shocks are renormalized or truncated.
The dashed blue line on the price plot is \(\mathbb E^Y[X(n)/X(0)]=1\). Dashed lines on the log plot are expected log prices. Exponentiating an expected log price does not give an expected price. Extremely large prices are marked as off scale; their log paths remain visible in full.






NoteWhat the sliders count



The counted trial is the down move in the Columbia preset, where \(a^X<a^Y\). The laboratory also permits \(a^X>a^Y\); then that trial raises the stock price and the terminating trial lowers it. The geometric count and likelihood formulas remain valid. The neutral label “counted trials” in the charts accommodates both directions.

title: The negative-binomial model
section: Linear information in the shock clock
text:
Linear information in the shock clock
For geometric parameters \(a,b\in(0,1)\), define
\[
\begin{aligned}
I(a,b)&=\log\frac{1-a}{1-b}\\
&\quad+\frac{a}{1-a}\log\frac ab.
\end{aligned}
\]
Relative entropy between the corresponding negative-binomial laws is \(nI(a,b)\). Applied to investor beliefs and the market,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^M_n\Vert\mathbb P^Y_n)\\
&\quad=nI(a^M,a^Y)\\
&\quad=n\times0.0849495.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is ideal expected log growth, attained if the payoff \(L_M(n)=\mathbb P^M_n/\mathbb P^Y_n\) can be implemented. The stock has its own separate information rate:
\[
\mathbb E^X\!\left[\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}\right]
=nI(a^X,a^Y).
\]
\[
\mathbb E^Y\!\left[\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}\right]
=-nI(a^Y,a^X).
\]
Under investor beliefs the stock’s expected log return instead equals
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E^M\!\left[\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}\right]\\
&\quad=n\{I(a^M,a^Y)-I(a^M,a^X)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This keeps ideal information, the stock’s induced law, and the investor’s actual assessment distinct.

title: The negative-binomial model
section: Wald’s identity: information per trial versus per shock
text:
Wald’s identity: information per trial versus per shock
The total number of binary trials is \(\tau(n)=Z(n)+n\). Under beliefs,
\[
\mathbb E^M[\tau(n)]=\frac{n}{1-a^M}=\frac32n.
\]
The one-trial log-likelihood increments are bounded and this stopping time has finite expectation. With \(d(a\Vert b)\) denoting Bernoulli relative entropy, as on the binomial page, Wald’s identity gives
\[
I(a^M,a^Y)=\frac{d(a^M\Vert a^Y)}{1-a^M}.
\]
Numerically, information per shock equals expected trials per shock times information per trial:
\[
0.0849495=\frac32\times0.0566330.
\]
The new clock creates no extra information. It packages a random number of observations into each unit of time.
If trading is available after every binary trial, rebalancing to the stock weight \(w=2/3\) produces an up multiplier \(4/3\) and a down multiplier \(2/3\). Its wealth at the end of a shock is exactly \(L_M=(4/3)(2/3)^G\), so it attains the full \(0.0849495\) nats.

title: The negative-binomial model
section: What changes when trading is restricted?
text:
What changes when trading is restricted?
Now permit trading only between completed shocks. A stock/cash portfolio held through one shock has payoff
\[
V_w=1+w(R-1).
\]
\[
\mathbb P^{V_w}=w\mathbb P^X+(1-w)\mathbb P^Y.
\]
There are infinitely many possible \(G\) values but only two traded securities. No single \(w\) matches the desired payoff in every state. The old binary weight \(2/3\) matches the mass of \(G=0\) and the combined tail \(G\geq1\); it does not match the individual tail outcomes.
The best fixed shock-level weight is \(w_{\mathrm{KL}}\approx0.745331\). Its expected log growth is \(0.0814623\), leaving a KL gap of \(0.0034872\) nats per shock. That gap is the gain available from the ideal within-shock rebalancing strategy in this frictionless example.
Compare exact KL, KL2, and quadratic hedging for the derivation, the full comparison table, and the distinction between ordinary squared error and a local approximation to information loss.






NoteOptional detail: what binary coarsening discards





Keep only the partition \(C=\{G=0,G\geq1\}\). Its market probabilities are \((1/2,1/2)\) and its belief probabilities are \((2/3,1/3)\). The coarse KL divergence is the same \(0.0566330\) as one binary trial.
The KL chain rule separates coarse information from conditional detail. Write \(M_c=\mathbb P^M(G\mid c)\) and \(Y_c=\mathbb P^Y(G\mid c)\) for the two conditional laws:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^M_G\Vert\mathbb P^Y_G)\\
&\quad=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^M_C\Vert\mathbb P^Y_C)\\
&\qquad+\sum_{c\in C}\mathbb P^M(c)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(M_c\Vert Y_c).
\end{aligned}
\]
The event \(G=0\) contains no remaining uncertainty. Conditional on \(G\geq1\), the shifted count \(G-1\) has the original geometric law under each measure. Hence
\[
D_{\mathrm{fine}}=D_{\mathrm{coarse}}+\frac13D_{\mathrm{fine}},
\]
\[
0.0849495=0.0566330+0.0283165.
\]
The coarsening loss \(0.0283165\) and the portfolio implementation gap \(0.0034872\) are different quantities. The first discards outcome detail; the second retains the full outcome space but restricts the available payoff.









NoteOptional detail: the likelihood principle





Suppose the observed data contain \(k\) counted down-type trials and \(n\) terminating up-type trials. For an unknown counted-trial probability \(a\), both a fixed-trial design and a design stopped at the \(n\)th terminating trial have likelihood proportional to \(a^k(1-a)^n\). Their combinatorial factors depend on the observed counts and design but not on \(a\).
Thus the realized likelihood ratio is the same in either design. This does not make their sampling distributions identical: procedures depending on unobserved outcomes, including fixed-design p-values, can differ. Evaluating the original binary wealth process at the \(n\)th terminating trial produces the negative-binomial wealth shown here.

title: Portfolio choice
text:
Portfolio choice has three inputs: what you believe, what you want, and what you can trade. Information theory provides a common way to describe them. Beliefs give a probability distribution; preferences select a payoff; the asset menu determines which payoff distributions are attainable.
Start with one bet and the payoff–probability correspondence if these ideas are new. This page maps the next steps.

title: Portfolio choice
text:
1. Specify the target
For expected log growth, investor beliefs \(\mathbb P^M\) are the target. With pricing law \(\mathbb P^Y\), the ideal unit-cost payoff is
\[
L_M=\frac{d\mathbb P^M}{d\mathbb P^Y}.
\]
It pays more in outcomes to which the investor assigns relatively more probability. This is a full-market benchmark; the required state claims may not trade.
Other preferences can select another target. In a complete market, utility maximization chooses a payoff \(G^U\), which induces \(\mathbb P^U=G^U\mathbb P^Y\). That payoff is log-optimal under its own induced law. The utility page explains CRRA, fractional Kelly, and why a constrained utility problem generally must still be solved using its original utility objective.
Hedging starts from a different input: a given nonnegative claim \(H\) with price \(H(0)=\mathbb E^Y[H]>0\). Its normalized payoff induces
\[
\frac{d\mathbb P^H}{d\mathbb P^Y}=\frac{H}{H(0)}.
\]
The claim supplies the target rather than an investor forecast. See pricing and hedging.

title: Portfolio choice
text:
2. Determine the attainable set
Suppose \(R_1,\ldots,R_K\) are nonnegative unit-cost traded returns with \(\mathbb E^Y[R_j]=1\). A long-only allocation \(a_j\geq0\), \(\sum_j a_j=1\), produces
\[
\begin{aligned}
G_a&=\sum_{j=1}^K a_jR_j,\\
\mathbb P^{V_a}&=\sum_{j=1}^K a_j\mathbb P^{X_j}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus long-only portfolios form a convex set of induced probability distributions. Additional position limits shrink the set. Intermediate rebalancing can enlarge the set of terminal payoffs relative to static trading; the available information and trading dates are part of the market specification.
The simplest illustration needs only three outcomes. In the incomplete football market, cash and a Win claim can match the desired Win probability but cannot independently choose the Draw/Loss split. The trinomial model shows the same geometry with a stock and cash.

title: Portfolio choice
section: 3. Measure the cost of imperfect implementation
text:
3. Measure the cost of imperfect implementation
For a positive unit-cost payoff \(G_a=d\mathbb P^{V_a}/d\mathbb P^Y\), the central identity is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E^M[\log G_a]
&=D(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^Y)\\
&\quad-D(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^{V_a}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Attainable log growth equals ideal information minus the KL gap. The first term is fixed once the beliefs and pricing law are specified. Maximizing expected log growth is therefore exactly the same as minimizing the second term over the attainable set. Complete markets can remove the gap; incomplete markets need not.
For finitely many states, this is a concave optimization problem in the portfolio weights:
\[
\max_{a\in\Delta_K}\sum_i\mathbb P^M(i)
\log\!\left(\sum_j a_jR_j(i)\right).
\]
The portfolio laboratory lets you change the target and the asset distributions and observe the resulting projection. The finite-state examples use positive pricing probabilities. A zero payoff in a state of positive subjective probability gives expected log growth \(-\infty\); the framework page states the support conditions for the general identity.






NoteWhich parts depend on the pricing law?





Keep beliefs, traded returns, and feasible portfolios fixed. Any equivalent pricing law \(Q\) that prices those returns gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(\mathbb P^M\Vert QG_a)
&=D(\mathbb P^M\Vert Q)\\
&\quad-\mathbb E^M[\log G_a].
\end{aligned}
\]
Changing \(Q\) shifts all exact KL gaps by the same constant. The optimal portfolio and attained expected log growth stay unchanged, while the ideal benchmark and absolute gaps can change. Quadratic approximations need not preserve this invariance. See the comparison of hedging criteria.
