title: Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
text:
The inverse Gaussian family supplies a second nonnegative additive driver alongside the gamma model. Its increments have a continuous, right-skewed density, while its paths increase through infinitely many jumps.
One interpretation comes from first-passage times. Let a Brownian motion with positive drift \(\gamma\) run until it first reaches height \(\delta t\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(s)&=W(s)+\gamma s,\\
I(t)&=\inf\{s\ge0:B(s)\ge\delta t\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
As the target height increases, the required waiting time forms an inverse Gaussian clock. Here \(t\) indexes the target level; \(s\) is the underlying Brownian clock. The likelihood model can be specified directly through the resulting distributions, without simulating that Brownian first-passage construction.

title: Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
section: Fix the additive scale; vary the tail parameter
text:
Fix the additive scale; vary the tail parameter
Use a common \(\delta>0\) and two positive parameters \(\gamma_X,\gamma_Y\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
I(t)&\sim\operatorname{IG}(\delta t,\gamma_X)
&&\text{under }\mathbb P^X,\\
I(t)&\sim\operatorname{IG}(\delta t,\gamma_Y)
&&\text{under }\mathbb P^Y.
\end{aligned}
\]
In this parameterization, for \(z>0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_j(z,t)
&=\frac{\delta t}{\sqrt{2\pi}}z^{-3/2}e^{\delta\gamma_jt}\\
&\quad\times\exp\!\left\{
-\frac{\delta^2t^2}{2z}
-\frac{\gamma_j^2z}{2}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The moments help interpret the parameters:
\[
E^j[I(t)]=\frac{\delta t}{\gamma_j},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}^j[I(t)]=\frac{\delta t}{\gamma_j^3}.
\]
Increasing \(\gamma_j\) reduces both the mean accumulation rate and its variance. Increasing the common scale \(\delta\) increases both linearly.

title: Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
section: A complicated density, a simple ratio
text:
A complicated density, a simple ratio
The common prefactor and the term involving \(1/z\) cancel in the ratio. Only an affine expression remains:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}&=aI(t)+bt,\\
a&=-\frac12(\gamma_X^2-\gamma_Y^2),\\
b&=\delta(\gamma_X-\gamma_Y).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}=\exp\{aI(t)+bt\}.
\]
The common scale \(\delta\) is what removes the nonlinear \(1/I(t)\) term. It is part of the model specification, not an accidental cancellation.

title: Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
section: Explore the clock and its price
text:
Explore the clock and its price
The figure fixes \(\gamma_Y=2\). Choose \(\delta\), the information rate and a price-jump direction; the matching \(\gamma_X\) follows from the KL formula. No drift or jump-size parameter is independently added after the densities have been selected.

The interactive model requires JavaScript. The default common scale is \(\delta=2\), the pricing parameter is \(\gamma_Y=2\) and the forward information rate is \(k=0.05\) nats per time unit.

title: Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
section: What the grid shows—and what it cannot
text:
What the grid shows—and what it cannot
Under \(\mathbb P^j\), the jump intensity density is
\[
\nu_j(dz)=\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
z^{-3/2}e^{-\gamma_j^2z/2}\,dz.
\]
The \(z^{-3/2}\) singularity is stronger than the gamma model’s \(z^{-1}\) singularity. Both produce infinitely many small jumps and finite total accumulated jump size on bounded time intervals.
Independent increments preserve the family: scales add while \(\gamma_j\) stays fixed. The widget samples the exact law \(\operatorname{IG}(\delta\Delta t,\gamma_j)\) at each grid interval. Its connecting segments visualize observed values and do not resolve the full infinite-activity path. Apparent smoothness at one plotting scale is not evidence of a diffusion.

title: Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
section: One construction, several forms of uncertainty
text:
One construction, several forms of uncertainty
Normal, Poisson, gamma and inverse Gaussian models all produce
\[
\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}=aZ(t)+bt.
\]
Their differences lie in the additive observation \(Z(t)\) and in the two laws assigned to it. The likelihood ratio handles the price normalization in every case. Independent drivers can later be combined by multiplying likelihood ratios, so their log prices and divergences add at the level of the joint observation.
Continue: return to linear information flow to compare the families, or to the framework to connect prices with portfolio choice.






NoteSource and conventions





Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, Chapter 5, “Inverse Gaussian family.” The book’s \(\operatorname{IG}(\delta t,\gamma)\) convention corresponds to the usual mean–shape parameters \(\mu=\delta t/\gamma\) and \(\lambda=(\delta t)^2\). Prices are in units of \(Y\).

title: Discrete hedging
text:
An option carries a probability density. A portfolio of stock and cash carries another. Hedging asks how closely the second can reproduce the first. Exact agreement means replication; a remaining difference records the exposures the available portfolio cannot match.
The options page plots distributions over observations at expiry. Here the question is local: what can a portfolio reproduce between now and the next trading date? All prices are in units of \(Y\), so the reference asset has value one.

title: Discrete hedging
section: A small example: the wealth constraint matters
text:
A small example: the wealth constraint matters
In the geometric-shock model, \(R_g=\tfrac32(\tfrac12)^g\) and \(q_g=2^{-(g+1)}\). A strike-one call pays
\[
\begin{aligned}
C&=(R-1)^+=\frac12\mathbf1_{\{G=0\}},\\
c&=\mathbb E^Y[C]=\frac14.
\end{aligned}
\]
Only the first outcome puts the call in the money. Among all stock-and-cash portfolios with the same cost \(c\), the unconstrained quadratic fit is
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_Q&=\frac7{16}R-\frac3{16},\\
\mathbb E^Y[(C-H_Q)^2]&=\frac1{128}.
\end{aligned}
\]
It has negative terminal wealth whenever \(G\geq2\). The squared-error criterion alone permits that result. Such a portfolio cannot induce a probability law.
If terminal wealth must remain nonnegative, write \(H_w=c[1+w(R-1)]\). The call’s induced law concentrates all probability at \(G=0\). Exact KL selects the all-stock boundary:
\[
\begin{aligned}
w_{\mathrm{KL}}&=1,\qquad H_{\mathrm{KL}}=\frac14R,\\
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^C\Vert\mathbb P^{H_{\mathrm{KL}}})&=\log\frac43.
\end{aligned}
\]
Quadratic fitting with the same nonnegative-wealth constraint also selects \(H=R/4\), with squared error \(1/56\). This distinguishes the choice of loss from the choice of admissible portfolios. See one mismatch, three criteria for an example where exact KL and the two quadratic losses select different positive portfolios.

title: Discrete hedging
text:
One trading interval
Suppose the stock is worth \(x=X(t)\) today, the call expires in \(\tau=T-t\) years, and the next rebalance is in \(h\) years, with \(0<h\leq\tau\). In the normal model, a standard normal shock \(z\) produces the stock multiplier
\[
R(h,z)=\exp\!\left\{\sigma\sqrt h\,z-\tfrac12\sigma^2h\right\}.
\]
Under the pricing measure, the shock has density \(q(z)=\varphi(z)\). The stock’s conditional density is therefore
\[
p(z)=R(h,z)\varphi(z).
\]
Both integrate to one: \(\mathbb E^Y[R(h,Z)]=1\). The plotted horizontal axis is the same standardized shock for every density. These are distributions over the next interval’s information, not histograms of hedging errors.
Write \(C(x,\tau)\) for the Black–Scholes call value at current stock price \(x\) and remaining maturity \(\tau\). At the next trading date, its value is \(C(xR(h,z),\tau-h)\). Consequently the call’s conditional density is
\[
c(z)=
\frac{C(xR(h,z),\tau-h)}{C(x,\tau)}
\varphi(z).
\]
Before expiry, the numerator is the remaining option value, rather than its terminal payoff. At \(h=\tau\), it becomes \((xR(h,z)-K)^+\). Conditional pricing ensures that this density also integrates to one.

title: Discrete hedging
section: A target that includes a reserve
text:
A target that includes a reserve
The explorer can hedge a call together with a fixed reserve \(B\geq0\) in \(Y\). Its current value is
\[
H=C(x,\tau)+B.
\]
Its density over the next interval becomes
\[
c_B(z)=
\frac{C(xR(h,z),\tau-h)+B}{H}
\varphi(z).
\]
The default uses \(B=K\): the terminal target is \((X(T)-K)^++K=\max(X(T),K)\), a stock position with a protected floor. This is also a put plus the stock by put–call parity.
Adding the reserve changes the target payoff as well as its price. It makes the target less concentrated in upside states; it does not supply a cost-free improvement to the original call hedge.
Spend a fraction \(w\) of the same budget \(H\) on stock and keep the rest in \(Y\). Hold that position until the next trading date. Its value and density are
\[
V(t+h,z)=H\{1-w+wR(h,z)\},
\]
\[
v(w,z)=\{1-w+wR(h,z)\}\varphi(z).
\]
This is a cost-weighted mixture of the stock and reference densities. The share holding is \(\Delta(t)=Hw/x\); the cost fraction \(w\) and the number of shares \(\Delta(t)\) are different quantities.

title: Discrete hedging
section: Move the hedge toward the target
text:
Move the hedge toward the target
Start with the call plus a reserve equal to the strike, then press Fit the density. Change the time to the next rebalance and compare the two curves. Finally select Call only to see why the positivity constraint matters.

The interactive density comparison requires JavaScript. For a stock price of 100, strike of 110, annual volatility 30%, and one year remaining, the call costs about 8.14 and its Black–Scholes delta is about 0.433 shares. With a 110-unit reserve the target costs 118.14; the corresponding delta cost fraction is about 0.367.

The fitted position minimizes the forward relative entropy
\[
w^\star=\underset{0\leq w\leq1}{\arg\min}\;
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(c_B\Vert v(w)),
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
&D_{\mathrm{KL}}(c_B\Vert v(w))\\
&\quad=\int c_B(z)\log\frac{c_B(z)}{v(w,z)}\,dz.
\end{aligned}
\]
Zero divergence means identical densities, hence identical next-date values for the same initial cost. Positive divergence measures the remaining mismatch in nats. It is also the loss of expected log performance, evaluated under the target measure, relative to holding the target itself.
The optimization is convex in \(w\). The figure compares its best value with the chosen position over several interval lengths. Shorter intervals change the local problem: they do not simply add more points to the same terminal distribution.

title: Discrete hedging
section: Why the call-only fit reaches a boundary
text:
Why the call-only fit reaches a boundary
In the normal model, the next stock multiplier can be arbitrarily close to zero or arbitrarily large. A position held unchanged over a finite interval must satisfy
\[
1-w+wR\geq0
\qquad\text{for every }R>0.
\]
With only stock and cash, that condition is exactly \(0\leq w\leq1\). Borrowing cash would give \(w>1\), and sufficiently large downward moves would then make the portfolio negative. Shorting the stock would fail in the other tail. A negative function cannot be used as a probability density.
For the default call without a reserve, Black–Scholes delta requires about 0.433 shares, costing about 43.34, while the call itself costs only 8.14. Its stock cost fraction is about 5.32: the rest is financed by borrowing. The finite-step positive-density fit cannot take that position. The Call only preset makes the restriction visible by putting the best admissible fit at the all-stock boundary.
This does not contradict continuous-time replication. A continuously rebalanced strategy changes its position as the stock moves. It is a different admissibility problem from a leveraged position left unchanged across a finite interval.

title: Discrete hedging
text:
Where Black–Scholes delta reappears
For the call plus a fixed reserve, the derivative with respect to stock price is still the call delta:
\[
\Delta^{\mathrm{BS}}(t)=\Phi(d(1)).
\]
\[
w^{\mathrm{BS}}=\frac{x\Phi(d(1))}{H}.
\]
The options page defines \(d(1)\) and derives the Black–Scholes formula from two normal tail probabilities. When this cost fraction is strictly inside the admissible interval, the short-interval KL fit approaches the same delta. The default reserve is large enough for this condition to hold. Press Fit the density, then reduce \(h\) to see the fitted share holding approach the delta benchmark.
The book also develops two quadratic hedges. For a positive normalized target payoff \(L\) and an equal-cost approximation \(V\), the target-centered KL approximation minimizes \(\tfrac12\mathbb E^Y[(V-L)^2/L]\); ordinary quadratic hedging minimizes \(\mathbb E^Y[(V-L)^2]\). Their finite-step positions need not agree. Under the local regularity and interior conditions, they approach delta as the interval shrinks in the normal model. The direct KL fit shown here retains the full logarithmic objective and its positivity restriction. The mean–variance page explains the two quadratic geometries and the limits needed to connect them.






NoteWhat is being calculated





The lab solves one conditional trading interval at the current stock price. A strategy on a trading grid repeats that calculation after each observed move, using the new stock price and remaining maturity. The graphs do not claim to show a complete multistep replication or a realized hedge profit.
The integrals use deterministic numerical quadrature over standard normal shocks, with a separate breakpoint at the strike when the interval reaches expiry. The plotted range contains nearly all the probability mass for these controls; numerical integration uses a wider range. Zero target density contributes zero to forward KL. The normal family and volatility range keep the integration well behaved.









NoteBook connection





Based on Chapter 6 of Jan Vecer’s Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective: local Kullback–Leibler projection, cost weights versus hedge shares, the normal model’s discrete call hedges, and the full-support positivity restriction. The reserve is an explicit target modification that makes an interior stock-and-cash comparison possible.

title: Gamma: accumulated activity
text:
The Poisson model counts isolated events. A gamma driver records a nonnegative amount of accumulated activity. It could represent an abstract operational clock or accumulated volume; the financial interpretation requires a model linking that quantity to the application.
The driver increases by jumps. Although its value at any fixed positive time has a continuous density, its paths are not continuous: a gamma process has infinitely many small jumps on every positive time interval.

title: Gamma: accumulated activity
text:
Common shape, different rates
Specify one additive driver \(G(t)\) under two measures:
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(t)&\sim\Gamma(\alpha t,\beta_X)
&&\text{under }\mathbb P^X,\\
G(t)&\sim\Gamma(\alpha t,\beta_Y)
&&\text{under }\mathbb P^Y.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(\alpha>0\) is the common shape rate. The parameters \(\beta_X,\beta_Y>0\) are rates, so the means and variances are
\[
E^j[G(t)]=\frac{\alpha t}{\beta_j},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}^j[G(t)]=\frac{\alpha t}{\beta_j^2}.
\]
For \(z>0\) and \(j\in\{X,Y\}\), the density is
\[
f_j(z,t)=\frac{\beta_j^{\alpha t}}{\Gamma(\alpha t)}
z^{\alpha t-1}e^{-\beta_jz}.
\]
The common power of \(z\) and the gamma-function factor cancel. The resulting price is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}
&=\left(\frac{\beta_X}{\beta_Y}\right)^{\alpha t}
e^{(\beta_Y-\beta_X)G(t)},\\
\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}&=aG(t)+bt,
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
a=\beta_Y-\beta_X,
\qquad b=\alpha\log\frac{\beta_X}{\beta_Y}.
\]
The common shape is essential for this affine expression. Different shape rates would leave an additional \(\log G(t)\) term.

title: Gamma: accumulated activity
text:
Explore the model
The figure fixes \(\beta_Y=2\). Choose the common shape rate, forward information rate and jump direction; the corresponding \(\beta_X\) is then determined. The displayed horizon is at least \(0.5\) and \(\alpha\ge2\), keeping the horizon density finite at zero. This is an exploration range, not a restriction on the mathematical gamma family.

The interactive model requires JavaScript. The default common shape rate is \(\alpha=3\), the pricing rate is \(\beta_Y=2\) and the forward information rate is \(k=0.05\) nats per time unit.

title: Gamma: accumulated activity
text:
Driver jumps become price jumps
For a driver jump of size \(\Delta G(t)>0\),
\[
\frac{X(t)}{X(t-)}=e^{a\Delta G(t)}.
\]
If \(\beta_X>\beta_Y\), the asset measure favors smaller amounts of activity. An upward jump in observed activity then produces a downward price jump, while \(b>0\) supplies the compensating deterministic component. If \(\beta_X<\beta_Y\), the price jumps upward and \(b<0\).
There is no positive interval free of all gamma jumps. The decomposition \(aG(t)+bt\) still separates the jump contribution from the deterministic contribution, but it should not be described as a succession of isolated jumps with empty waiting periods.
The jump intensity density under measure \(\mathbb P^j\) is
\[
\nu_j(dz)=\alpha z^{-1}e^{-\beta_jz}\,dz,
\qquad z>0.
\]
Its integral diverges near zero, giving infinite activity. The integral of jump size against this density is finite, so total accumulated jump size is finite over bounded intervals.

title: Gamma: accumulated activity
text:
Information accumulated per unit time
Taking the mean of the affine log likelihood gives the divergence between the two observation laws at horizon \(t\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(\mathbb P^X\Vert\mathbb P^Y)&=k_Xt,\\
k_X&=\alpha\left[
\log\frac{\beta_X}{\beta_Y}
-1+\frac{\beta_Y}{\beta_X}\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Reversing the two measures gives
\[
k_Y=\alpha\left[
\log\frac{\beta_Y}{\beta_X}
-1+\frac{\beta_X}{\beta_Y}\right].
\]
The expected log-price slopes are \(+k_X\) under \(\mathbb P^X\) and \(-k_Y\) under \(\mathbb P^Y\). The price ratio itself remains a mean-one martingale under \(\mathbb P^Y\).

title: Gamma: accumulated activity
section: From discrete blocks to an additive clock
text:
From discrete blocks to an additive clock
The negative-binomial model sums independent geometric blocks. Gamma laws supply a continuous-valued analogue: independent gamma variables with the same rate add their shape parameters,
\[
\begin{gathered}
\Gamma(\alpha s,\beta)+\Gamma(\alpha t,\beta)\\
\overset{d}{=}\ \Gamma(\alpha(s+t),\beta).
\end{gathered}
\]
For integer shape, a gamma variable is a sum of exponential waiting times. Positive noninteger shapes extend that family consistently to every time increment. The simulation uses these exact increment distributions; the connecting segments do not reproduce the infinitely many individual jumps.
Continue: the inverse Gaussian model gives another additive positive clock, with a different density and a stronger small-jump singularity.






NoteSource and conventions





Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, Chapter 5, “Gamma family.” Shape–rate convention: \(\Gamma(s,\beta)\) has mean \(s/\beta\). All prices are in units of \(Y\); \(\mathbb P^X\) and an investor’s \(\mathbb P^M\) are distinct unless explicitly identified.

title: Information through time
text:
The static framework connects a payoff to a probability distribution. Time introduces two further questions: how does new information change the price, and how does an investor adapt as outcomes arrive?
These questions share a likelihood language, but concern different objects. A price process compares two consistent probability laws through time. An adaptive allocation also specifies a learning rule, a trading rule, and the capital available for future decisions.

title: Information through time
section: From one payoff to a price process
text:
From one payoff to a price process
Start with two equivalent probability laws on the same evolving observations. Their likelihood-ratio process is a positive martingale under the reference law. Expressing prices in units of the reference asset incorporates the numeraire convention from the outset.
The two ways to build a market page explains the connection with the classical route: begin with price dynamics, then recover compatible pricing probabilities. The binomial model makes both directions explicit.

title: Information through time
section: A companion chapter: linear information flows
text:
A companion chapter: linear information flows
Independent increments in suitable exponential families give particularly transparent models. The log price is affine in an accumulating statistic, and expected information grows linearly in the stated clock. This is a useful subclass of price models; the general payoff–probability correspondence does not require linear information flow.
The separate Linear information flows chapter contains six model sections: binomial, negative binomial, normal, Poisson, gamma, and inverse Gaussian. Its overview specifies what accumulates and which parameters stay common. The normal example recovers geometric Brownian motion; the jump examples illustrate different patterns of information arrival.
Suggested route: binomial → negative binomial → linear information flow. For continuous-time examples, start with normal / GBM, then explore the remaining families in the catalogue.

title: Information through time
section: The trading clock changes what can be implemented
text:
The trading clock changes what can be implemented
Observing every binary move and trading after every move is a different opportunity set from trading only before and after a completed shock. The negative-binomial example holds the underlying sequence of trials fixed and makes this distinction visible.
In the Columbia example, the resulting growth gap measures the value of the unavailable intermediate rebalancing. The comparison of three hedging criteria shows the portfolios and the numerical decomposition.

title: Information through time
text:
Learning and capital commitment
Under full commitment in the specified prediction-market setting, relative wealth evolves like Bayesian model weights. Partial commitment changes that recursion. Keeping capital in reserve and preserving accumulated evidence are distinct decisions.
The Bayesian learning and commitment page develops this connection, including the role of prefunded restarts. The Oxford presentation provides the broader computational context.

title: Bayesian learning and adaptation
text:
A probability forecast can define an investment payoff. If several forecasting models each retain their own bankroll, good relative predictions increase their wealth and their influence on the next price. Under full commitment, the wealth update is exactly Bayes’ rule.
The next question is different: what happens when a model that fitted the past stops fitting the present? Reducing the next stake limits exposure, but accumulated wealth still carries the history. Adaptation requires a mechanism for evaluating recent evidence separately.
This page develops the ideas in the Oxford presentation, using normalized probabilities and returns in reference-asset units.

title: Bayesian learning and adaptation
text:
Forecasts become separate model funds
Before observation \(X_{t+1}\), model \(i\) supplies a predictive distribution \(p_{i,t}\) and has bankroll \(B_{i,t}>0\). Let \(m_t\) be a common positive pricing distribution. Investing the whole bankroll according to the forecast gives
\[
\frac{B_{i,t+1}}{B_{i,t}}
=\frac{p_{i,t}(X_{t+1})}{m_t(X_{t+1})}.
\]
The gross return is a likelihood ratio. The log return is the model’s log score minus the market’s log score. A portfolio of these funds, held with value weights \(\pi_{i,t}\), induces the mixture forecast \(\sum_i\pi_{i,t}p_{i,t}\).
Forecasts, weights, and commitments must be fixed before the next observation. Selecting the winning forecast afterwards would instead require a best-of claim with its own price.

title: Bayesian learning and adaptation
text:
Clearing uses committed capital
Suppose each model commits a fraction \(\lambda_{i,t}\in[0,1]\) and leaves the rest in the reference asset. Write
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{i,t}&=\frac{B_{i,t}}{\sum_jB_{j,t}},\\
\bar\lambda_t&=\sum_i\pi_{i,t}\lambda_{i,t}>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
In a common Arrow-ticket mechanism, statewise budget balance determines the quote
\[
m_t^\lambda(x)
=\sum_i\frac{\pi_{i,t}\lambda_{i,t}}{\bar\lambda_t}p_{i,t}(x).
\]
The coefficients are shares of committed capital, which need not be shares of total wealth. Settlement gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{B_{i,t+1}}{B_{i,t}}
&=1-\lambda_{i,t}\\
&\quad+\lambda_{i,t}\frac{p_{i,t}(X_{t+1})}{m_t^\lambda(X_{t+1})}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Total bankroll is unchanged by settlement within the pool, for every outcome. Individual accounts gain or lose. The quoted mixture is unique within this specified common-ticket, statewise balanced mechanism; this is not a uniqueness claim about every possible market design.

title: Bayesian learning and adaptation
text:
Full commitment gives Bayes’ rule
When every \(\lambda_{i,t}=1\), the quote is the wealth-weighted predictive mixture,
\[
m_t(x)=\sum_i\pi_{i,t}p_{i,t}(x).
\]
Since total bankroll is conserved, the updated wealth share is
\[
\pi_{i,t+1}
=\frac{\pi_{i,t}p_{i,t}(X_{t+1})}
{\sum_j\pi_{j,t}p_{j,t}(X_{t+1})}.
\]
This is the Bayesian posterior update for model weights. The equivalence is algebraic: it follows from likelihood-ratio returns and retaining gains within each model account.






NoteA two-model update



Two models start with equal wealth and predict Win probabilities \(0.7\) and \(0.4\). The clearing Win price is \(0.55\). After a Win, their wealth shares become
\[
\begin{gathered}
\left(\frac{0.5(0.7)}{0.55},\frac{0.5(0.4)}{0.55}\right)\\
=\left(\frac7{11},\frac4{11}\right).
\end{gathered}
\]
After a Loss they would instead become \((1/3,2/3)\). A model gains relative influence when the observation was more likely under its forecast.








NoteThe information in a mixture





If a latent model index \(\Theta\) has conditional distribution \(\pi_t\), and the next observation has conditional law \(p_{i,t}\) given \(\Theta=i\), then
\[
\sum_i\pi_{i,t}D(p_{i,t}\Vert m_t)
=I(\Theta;X_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t).
\]
The average divergence from each model to the predictive mixture is the mutual information between the model identity and the next observation. This interpretation uses the specified joint probabilistic model; it does not establish that any candidate is the true data-generating mechanism.

title: Bayesian learning and adaptation
Bayesian learning and adaptation
section: Capital can remain attached to an obsolete model
text:
Capital can remain attached to an obsolete model
Suppose two fixed, strictly positive distributions \(p\ne q\) on a finite outcome space are available. Observations are independent, first i.i.d. from \(p\) for \(\tau\) periods, then i.i.d. from \(q\) permanently. Both accounts start with positive wealth and use a fixed common commitment fraction \(\lambda\in(0,1]\).
The old model can enter the new regime with a large wealth advantage. Even though the new observations now favor \(q\), the clearing price can remain close to \(p\) while that advantage is worked off. Under this switch model, the catch-up time \(H_\tau\) satisfies
\[
\frac{H_\tau}{\tau}\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}\kappa_\lambda(p,q).
\]
For full commitment,
\[
\kappa_1(p,q)=\frac{D(p\Vert q)}{D(q\Vert p)}.
\]
The numerator measures the earlier evidence accumulated in favor of \(p\); the denominator measures how quickly new observations favor \(q\). Fixed partial commitment changes the coefficient but leaves recovery proportional to the length of the old regime in this setting.






NoteThe coefficient under partial commitment





Put \(r_\lambda=(1-\lambda)p+\lambda q\). Under the finite-state, independent permanent-switch assumptions above,
\[
\kappa_\lambda(p,q)
=\frac{D(p\Vert r_\lambda)}
{D(q\Vert p)-D(q\Vert r_\lambda)}.
\]
For fixed distinct positive \(p,q\), \(\kappa_\lambda=\lambda/2+O(\lambda^2)\) as \(\lambda\downarrow0\). This is a statement about the asymptotic lock-in coefficient, not a general guarantee that taking arbitrarily small stakes gives fast or useful learning. A smaller commitment also slows the recovery of a given wealth deficit.

title: Bayesian learning and adaptation
text:
Restart accounts isolate recent evidence
A restart account asks a local question: did a candidate forecast predict a specified recent window better than the incumbent benchmark?
Let \(p_{0,t}\) be the strictly positive benchmark forecast and \(p_{1,t},\ldots,p_{K,t}\) the candidates. A pooling vector \(a\in\Delta_K\) gives the forecast \(q_{a,t}=\sum_i a_i p_{i,t}\). An account starting at observation \(s\) and active for \(d\) observations has benchmark-relative wealth
\[
L_t^{s,d,a}
=\prod_{u=s}^{\min\{t,s+d-1\}}
\frac{q_{a,u-1}(X_u)}{p_{0,u-1}(X_u)}.
\]
The empty product is one before the account starts. During the window, it accumulates relative evidence. After expiry, its wealth stays in the benchmark and its relative value is frozen.







Stage
What the account measures




Before \(s\)
No evidence yet; capital remains in the benchmark


From \(s\) through \(s+d-1\)
Likelihood evidence on the selected window


After the window
The completed window’s evidence, with no further factors

title: Bayesian learning and adaptation
section: Pay for the search before seeing its outcomes
text:
Pay for the search before seeing its outcomes
Choosing the best start time or model after observing the data would overstate the evidence. Instead, assign initial capital fractions \(\gamma_{s,d}\geq0\) to windows in advance, with \(\sum_{s,d}\gamma_{s,d}\leq1\), and a probability prior \(\nu_{s,d}\) over pooling weights. The combined process is
\[
\begin{aligned}
U_t^{s,d}&=\int_{\Delta_K}L_t^{s,d,a}\,\nu_{s,d}(da),\\
E_t&=c+\sum_{s,d}\gamma_{s,d}U_t^{s,d},\\
c&=1-\sum_{s,d}\gamma_{s,d}.
\end{aligned}
\]
If the benchmark kernels \(p_{0,t}\) are the true conditional law under the null, and the candidate forecasts are normalized and determined before each observation, \((E_t)\) is a nonnegative martingale starting at one. Ville’s inequality gives
\[
\mathbb P_0\!\left(\sup_tE_t\geq\frac1\delta\right)\leq\delta.
\]
This is an anytime false-alarm bound under that specified null. An alarm is evidence that the monitored forecasts outperform the benchmark. By itself, it does not identify an abrupt structural change; benchmark misspecification can also produce sustained relative evidence.






NoteImplementation and recovery guarantees





The statistical search can contain many windows and pooling weights without requiring one distinct traded security for each. When the candidate likelihood-return funds and benchmark are available, their time-dependent holdings can be consolidated using posterior mean weights into the \(K\) candidate funds plus the benchmark.
The associated research obtains a logarithmic recovery scale for an appropriately prefunded restart design under its stated switch model, conditional on no prior alarm. This requires the candidate family and priors to support the new regime, suitable window funding, and a positive relative growth advantage. It is not a uniform recovery guarantee for arbitrary data, forecasts, or funding rules.

title: The binomial model
text:
Each period has two outcomes, \(H\) and \(T\): an up move and a down move in our running example. Three laws have different jobs: \(\mathbb P^Y\) prices payoffs, \(\mathbb P^X\) is induced by the traded stock, and \(\mathbb P^M\) describes investor beliefs. The stock is the investor’s log-optimal holding only when \(\mathbb P^M=\mathbb P^X\).
Every identity on the framework page has an explicit two-state form. We use the same numbers as the Columbia presentation:
Here \(R=\mathbb P^X/\mathbb P^Y\) and \(L_M=\mathbb P^M/\mathbb P^Y\). All prices and returns are in units of the reference asset \(Y\); interest and discounting are absorbed in that choice. When \(Y\) is money delivered at the horizon, the reference security is the corresponding bond.
This is the first worked example of likelihoods and price dynamics: the two approaches describe the same market, but start with different primitives.

title: The binomial model
text:
Two probabilities, two multipliers
Write \(p=\mathbb P^X(H)\) and \(q=\mathbb P^Y(H)\), with \(p,q\in(0,1)\). Likelihood-ratio pricing, \(X(1)/X(0)=\mathbb P^X/\mathbb P^Y\), gives the \(H\) and \(T\) multipliers directly (up and down, respectively, when \(p>q\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
u&=\frac{p}{q},\\
d&=\frac{1-p}{1-q}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The corresponding asset return is
\[
\frac{X(1)}{X(0)}=
\begin{cases} u & H,\\ d & T.\end{cases}
\]
There are two martingale conditions, one for each choice of numeraire. Under the reference-asset measure \(\mathbb P^Y\), the normalized price of \(X\) has expectation one:
\[
\begin{aligned}
q\,u+(1-q)\,d
&=p+(1-p)\\
&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Under the asset measure \(\mathbb P^X\), the normalized price of \(Y\) in units of \(X\) is the reciprocal return. It also has expectation one:
\[
\begin{aligned}
p\,\frac1u+(1-p)\,\frac1d
&=q+(1-q)\\
&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first condition identifies \(q\) from nonconstant price multipliers; the second identifies \(p\). Thus \(p\) is the probability associated with the asset numeraire, not an independently supplied forecast. The investor’s forecast is \(m=\mathbb P^M(H)\). In the example, \(q=1/2\), \(p=3/4\), and \(m=2/3\).
The classical one-period model runs the other way. It postulates \(u\) and \(d\) and derives the pricing probabilities from these martingale conditions. Solving them gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
q&=\frac{1-d}{u-d},\\
p&=\frac{u(1-d)}{u-d}=u\,q.
\end{aligned}
\]
The map \((p,q)\mapsto(u,d)\) sends \(\{0<q<p<1\}\) one-to-one onto \(\{0<d<1<u\}\). Read backwards, the classical no-arbitrage condition \(d<1<u\) corresponds to two interior probabilities ordered so that \(H\) is the up move. With \(p<q\), the price directions reverse: \(H\) is the down move and \(0<u<1<d\). When \(p=q\), \(u=d=1\): the asset has the reference asset’s return. In that degenerate case the return identifies neither probability, and the inverse formulas are undefined. Equal multipliers different from one imply deterministic arbitrage in units of \(Y\), under the frictionless borrowing and short-selling assumptions.
With two states, cash and a nonconstant asset span all payoffs, which is why these conditions identify the two measures uniquely. The trinomial model shows what changes when there are three states and only two traded assets.




Interactive figure. It needs JavaScript.



Figure 1: One period of the asset \(X\) in units of \(Y\). Start from the probabilities or from the multipliers; the other pair follows in the nondegenerate no-arbitrage region. Both numeraire martingale conditions appear below the diagram. Multipliers on the same side of 1, or one equal to 1 and the other different, imply arbitrage when both scenarios are possible. The figure distinguishes these cases from the fair constant return \(u=d=1\). Editing a probability in a later figure switches this figure to probability mode and explains the change.

title: The binomial model
text:
Replication: shares and probability weights
The classical delta hedge and likelihood matching are the same calculation in different coordinates. To replicate terminal wealth \(V(1)\), hold \(\Delta\) shares of \(X\) and the remaining budget in \(Y\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta&=\frac{V(1,H)-V(1,T)}{X(1,H)-X(1,T)},\\
B&=V(0)-\Delta X(0).
\end{aligned}
\]
The initial fraction of the budget invested in the stock is \(w=\Delta X(0)/V(0)\). Normalized terminal wealth and its induced probability law satisfy
\[
V_w=\frac{V(1)}{V(0)}=1+w(R-1).
\]
\[
\mathbb P^V=w\mathbb P^X+(1-w)\mathbb P^Y.
\]
For the target \(\mathbb P^V=\mathbb P^M\), the \(H\) equation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
w&=\frac{m-q}{p-q}\\
&=\frac{2/3-1/2}{3/4-1/2}=\frac23.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(\Delta=(2/3)V(0)/X(0)\), \(B=V(0)/3\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
V_{2/3}(H)&=\frac43,\\
V_{2/3}(T)&=\frac23.
\end{aligned}
\]
The line \(V_w=1+w(R-1)\) passes through both desired payoffs. With two states and two independent securities, the target is attainable exactly. The mixture is convex for \(0\leq w\leq1\); borrowing or short selling can extend it when terminal wealth remains nonnegative.

title: The binomial model
text:
Every position on one curve
Write \(d(a\Vert b)\) for the relative entropy between Bernoulli laws with probabilities \(a\) and \(b\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
d(a\Vert b)
&=a\log\frac ab\\
&\quad +(1-a)\log\frac{1-a}{1-b}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The usual conventions apply: a zero-probability term contributes zero, while positive probability divided by zero gives infinite divergence.
Let the investor’s model be \(\mathbb P^M(H)=m\). With two scenarios a nonnegative portfolio \(V\) of positive price is determined, up to scale, by \(v=\mathbb P^V(H)\), the fraction of wealth spent on the \(H\) claim. The stock fraction \(w\) in the replication section gives
\[
v=wp+(1-w)q.
\]
Thus the \(v\)-curve below and the payoff line \(V_w=1+w(R-1)\) describe the same positions in different coordinates. The portfolio’s expected log return under the investor’s model is
\[
\begin{aligned}
g(v)
&=m\log\frac{v}{q}\\
&\quad +(1-m)\log\frac{1-v}{1-q}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The information decomposition becomes
\[
g(v)=d(m\Vert q)-d(m\Vert v).
\]
Three points on the curve have names. At \(v=q\) the investor holds the reference asset and \(g=0\). At \(v=p\) she holds the asset \(X\). At \(v=m\) the curve peaks at \(d(m\Vert q)\), and the shortfall of any other position is exactly \(d(m\Vert v)\). Every strictly positive portfolio is log-optimal for the model it implies, and for no other in this unconstrained two-state market.
In the running example, the replicated target earns
\[
\begin{aligned}
g^*&=\frac23\log\frac43+\frac13\log\frac23\\
&\approx0.0566330\ \text{nats per trial}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Holding the stock alone earns \(\frac23\log(3/2)+\frac13\log(1/2)\approx0.0392610\). The investor and stock laws differ, so simply buying the stock does not maximize this investor’s expected log growth.
For \(\gamma\ge1\), risk aversion moves the position from \(m\) back toward \(q\), in one of two ways. Fractional Kelly keeps a cash reserve:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f&=1/\gamma,\\
v_f&=(1-f)\,q+f\,m.
\end{aligned}
\]
CRRA utility instead tempers the measure. Set \(\alpha=1/\gamma\) and form the weights
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_H&=m^\alpha q^{1-\alpha},\\
a_T&=(1-m)^\alpha(1-q)^{1-\alpha}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The optimal \(H\) weight is
\[
v_\gamma=\frac{a_H}{a_H+a_T}.
\]
For \(0<m<1\) both families sweep the same segment between \(q\) and \(m\), including cash as a limit as \(\gamma\to\infty\). They generally traverse it at different rates: the same numerical \(\gamma\) can give different positions, while a change of \(\gamma\) can match them. With three or more states they generally trace different curves in the simplex, arithmetic against normalized geometric interpolation. Boundary beliefs give another distinction: set \(\mathbb P^M(H)=0\) in the figure. For every finite \(\gamma\), CRRA keeps that zero, while fractional Kelly with \(\gamma>1\) assigns positive weight through its cash reserve. The utility and risk-aversion page develops the general construction.




Interactive figure. It needs JavaScript.



Figure 2: Expected log return under \(\mathbb P^M\) of every two-state position. The red segment is the mismatch divergence. The separate marker lanes below the curve keep all six positions identifiable even when they coincide; vertical leaders connect the lane markers to their positions on the curve. The ring and diamond denote fractional Kelly and CRRA at the chosen \(\gamma\). The key reports each position and its growth numerically.

title: The binomial model
text:
Many periods
Repeat the period independently and let \(S(n)\) count the \(H\) outcomes after \(n\) periods. Likelihood-ratio pricing at time \(n\) gives
\[
\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}
=\Big(\frac pq\Big)^{S(n)}
\Big(\frac{1-p}{1-q}\Big)^{n-S(n)}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}=u^{S(n)}d^{\,n-S(n)}.
\]
The binomial coefficients in \(\mathbb P^X\) and \(\mathbb P^Y\) cancel. The price depends on the path only through the sufficient statistic \(S(n)\), and its logarithm is affine in it:
\[
\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}=a\,S(n)+b\,n.
\]
Here the coefficients are
\[
\begin{aligned}
a&=\log(u/d),\\
b&=\log d.
\end{aligned}
\]
Write \(D^{X,Y}(n)\) for the divergence between the laws of \(S(n)\) under the two measures. Independence gives
\[
D^{X,Y}(n)=n\,d(p\Vert q).
\]
The investor’s desired likelihood payoff has the same form with \(p\) replaced by \(m\). It is implemented by rebalancing to \(w=2/3\) after each trial in our example, and its expected log growth under \(\mathbb P^M\) is \(n\,d(m\Vert q)=n\times0.0566330\).
This is linear information flow: independent observations add information, while wealth compounds multiplicatively.
Under \(\mathbb P^Y\) the price \(X(t)/X(0)\) is a nonnegative martingale with mean one. Ville’s inequality then gives, for every horizon \(n\),
\[
\mathbb P^Y\Big(\max_{t\le n}\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}\ge\frac1\alpha\Big)\le\alpha .
\]
For \(0<\alpha<1\), the price path of \(X\) is therefore an anytime-valid test of the market’s model against the asset’s: one may stop the moment \(X\) has multiplied by \(1/\alpha\), and the probability of ever crossing under \(\mathbb P^Y\) is at most \(\alpha\). If \(p\ne q\), then under \(\mathbb P^X\) the long-run log growth is the strictly positive one-period divergence, so the threshold is eventually crossed with probability one over an unbounded horizon. If \(p=q\), wealth stays constant and no such rejection occurs.




Interactive figure. It needs JavaScript.



Figure 3: Top: the laws of \(S(n)\) under the two measures, shown as filled green bars for \(\mathbb P^X\) and blue outlines for \(\mathbb P^Y\), followed by the log price as a function of \(S(n)\). The outlines remain visible when the laws coincide. Bottom: eight simulated paths under each measure, with the expected log price as dashed lines and the rejection threshold \(\log(1/\alpha)\). Changing \(p\) or \(q\) reuses the same random numbers, so the paths deform rather than redraw. Ville’s bound concerns the true crossing probability; the reported Monte Carlo fraction is an estimate and can fluctuate above the bound.

title: The binomial model
text:
Same observations, different trading opportunities
Now group the trials into cycles: down moves followed by the first up. If trading remains possible after every binary step, the same \(w=2/3\) strategy still implements the belief likelihood. If trading is permitted only between completed cycles, a single stock/cash position need not match every possible cycle outcome.
The negative-binomial model develops this change of clock. The comparison of portfolio criteria then measures the resulting information gap and compares exact KL, its quadratic approximation, and quadratic hedging.

title: Two ways to build a market
text:
The classical approach starts with asset prices and asks which probability measure makes their discounted evolution a martingale. The likelihood approach can start with the measures and obtain the price moves from their ratios. The mathematical connection is exact. What changes is the choice of inputs.
All prices below are in units of a strictly positive reference asset \(Y\). Thus \(Y\) itself has constant value one.
crumbs: Two ways to build a market

title: Two ways to build a market
text:
Start with the dynamics
Specify a finite set of possible states, a finite trading horizon, and the prices and payoffs of the traded assets. Assume frictionless trading, unrestricted borrowing and short selling, no intermediate dividends, and that every state is possible. An arbitrage is a self-financing strategy with zero initial cost, nonnegative terminal payoff in every state, and a positive payoff in at least one state.
The fundamental theorem of asset pricing, in this finite, discrete setting, says:






NoteExistence: no arbitrage



There is no arbitrage if and only if there exists a probability measure \(\mathbb P^Y\), positive on every possible state, under which every traded price in units of \(Y\) is a martingale.


For a one-period asset with gross returns \(R_i\) this gives two equations:
\[
\sum_i q_i=1,
\qquad
\sum_i q_i R_i=1,
\]
where \(q_i=\mathbb P^Y(\omega_i)>0\). Over several periods the pricing equation becomes conditional:
\[
\mathbb E^Y[X(t+1)\mid\mathcal F_t]=X(t).
\]
These equations identify a pricing measure when their solution is unique. Otherwise, they identify a family of admissible measures. The investor’s subjective probabilities \(\mathbb P^M\) need not be the pricing probabilities.






NoteUniqueness: completeness



In the same finite, arbitrage-free setting, the market is complete if and only if its equivalent martingale measure is unique. Completeness means that trading the available assets can replicate every terminal payoff.


No arbitrage ensures that a consistent pricing rule exists. Completeness is the additional property that makes every contingent payoff replicable and its price unique. Portfolio constraints can further restrict what an investor can implement.

title: Two ways to build a market
section: Now read the same market through likelihoods
text:
Now read the same market through likelihoods
Fix a pricing measure \(\mathbb P^Y\) and a strictly positive traded asset \(X\). At the terminal date define
\[
\mathbb P^X(\omega)
=\frac{X(T,\omega)}{X(0)}\,\mathbb P^Y(\omega).
\]
The martingale pricing equation says exactly that these weights sum to one. Rearranging gives
\[
\frac{X(T,\omega)}{X(0)}
=\frac{\mathbb P^X(\omega)}{\mathbb P^Y(\omega)}.
\]
Conversely, specify two positive probability distributions. Their ratio defines a unit-cost return whose expectation under \(\mathbb P^Y\) is one. For a process, use their consistent restrictions to the information available at each date:
\[
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}
=\left.\frac{d\mathbb P^X}{d\mathbb P^Y}\right|_{\mathcal F_t}.
\]
The conditional likelihood ratio is a \(\mathbb P^Y\)-martingale. Positive prices also permit the reverse direction:
\[
\frac{X(0)}{X(t)}
=\left.\frac{d\mathbb P^Y}{d\mathbb P^X}\right|_{\mathcal F_t},
\]
which is a martingale under \(\mathbb P^X\). In financial terms, the price of \(Y\) in units of \(X\) is fair under the \(X\)-numeraire measure, just as the price of \(X\) in units of \(Y\) is fair under the \(Y\)-numeraire measure.
crumbs: Two ways to build a market

title: Two ways to build a market
text:
Two states identify the measure
For the nondegenerate binomial model, assume \(u>1>d>0\). The pricing equation is
\[
qu+(1-q)d=1.
\]
There is a unique solution:
\[
q=\frac{1-d}{u-d},
\qquad p=uq.
\]
Starting from \(p\) and \(q\) instead recovers the same moves:
\[
u=\frac pq,
\qquad d=\frac{1-p}{1-q}.
\]
With two states and two independent traded payoffs, the stock and the reference asset span every payoff. This is why the pricing measure is unique. If both returns equal one, that independence is lost; the market cannot distinguish the two states through these assets.
Explore both directions in the binomial model →

title: Two ways to build a market
section: Three states reveal what is missing
text:
Three states reveal what is missing
Add a middle state while keeping only the stock and the reference asset. For the book’s returns
\[
R=\left(\frac32,1,\frac12\right),
\]
all the following measures price the same stock:
\[
\mathbb P^Y=(t,1-2t,t),
\qquad 0<t<\frac12.
\]
For each such choice, the associated asset measure is
\[
\mathbb P^X
=\left(\frac{3t}{2},1-2t,\frac t2\right).
\]
The return vector alone does not select \(t\). Another traded claim, a calibration target, or an explicit modeling criterion can supply additional information.
Choosing the measures directly makes the pricing identities automatic. It does not make the measures observable or make missing payoffs tradable. A model still needs a way to select its inputs, and portfolio choice still takes place within the span of the available assets.

The binomial model can be built either from repeated up/down moves or from two binomial laws whose likelihood ratio produces those moves. Replacing the binomial count by a negative-binomial count gives a new price model through the same construction.

title: One mismatch, three criteria
text:
The desired payoff can be clear even when trading cannot produce it. The investor supplies a target distribution; stock and cash span a smaller set of distributions. The choice of loss determines which attainable portfolio comes closest.
This page continues the binomial example and the negative-binomial trading clock. All payoffs are expressed in units of the reference asset \(Y\) and normalized to initial cost one.

title: One mismatch, three criteria
section: The same binary tree, a different trading rule
text:
The same binary tree, a different trading rule
In the binary model, stock returns are \(u=3/2\) and \(d=1/2\). The up probabilities are \(1/2\) under the pricing law and \(2/3\) under the investor’s beliefs. Rebalancing a stock fraction \(w=2/3\) after every step produces the desired likelihood payoff.
Now let one trading period contain \(G\) down moves followed by the first up move. You may trade before and after the completed shock, but not during it. For \(g=0,1,\ldots\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
q_g&=\mathbb P^Y(G=g)=2^{-(g+1)},\\
m_g&=\mathbb P^M(G=g)=\frac23\left(\frac13\right)^g.
\end{aligned}
\]
The stock return and desired payoff are
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_g&=\frac32\left(\frac12\right)^g,\\
L_{M,g}&=\frac{m_g}{q_g}=\frac43\left(\frac23\right)^g.
\end{aligned}
\]
The stock’s law is \(p^X_g=q_gR_g=\tfrac34(\tfrac14)^g\). Holding a stock fraction \(w\) unchanged throughout the shock gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
V_w&=1+w(R-1),\\
v_g(w)&=q_gV_w(g).
\end{aligned}
\]
This is an affine payoff in \(R\). The desired \(L_M\) is nonlinear in \(R\), so no single stock-and-cash holding matches it in every state. Strictly positive wealth in every state requires \(-2<w\leq1\). The explorer focuses on \(0\leq w\leq1\), which contains all three optima in the examples below.
At \(w=2/3\), the portfolio matches the probability of \(G=0\) and the total probability of \(G\geq1\). It does not match the individual outcomes inside that tail. This is why the binary solution need not solve the completed-shock problem.

title: One mismatch, three criteria
section: Three ways to measure the remaining mismatch
text:
Three ways to measure the remaining mismatch
Write \(e_g=v_g(w)-m_g\). Exact information loss is
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(w)&=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(m\Vert v(w))\\
&=\sum_gm_g\log\frac{m_g}{v_g(w)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
It is exactly equivalent to maximizing expected log growth:
\[
\mathbb E^M[\log V_w]=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(m\Vert q)-D(w).
\]
Two quadratic alternatives are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{KL}_2(w)
&=\frac12\sum_g\frac{e_g^2}{m_g}\\
&=\frac12\mathbb E^Y\left[\frac{(V_w-L_M)^2}{L_M}\right],
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
Q(w)=\sum_g\frac{e_g^2}{q_g}
=\mathbb E^Y[(V_w-L_M)^2].
\]
The target-centered \(\operatorname{KL}_2\) is the second-order expansion of exact KL when the relative mismatch \((V_w-L_M)/L_M\) is small with suitable integrability. Its factor of \(1/2\) comes from that expansion. Ordinary quadratic hedging weights payoff errors using the pricing law; we define its loss \(Q\) without a factor of \(1/2\) throughout. Rescaling a loss by a positive constant changes its value but not its minimizing portfolio. The two quadratic criteria have different denominators; exact KL also has a different, logarithmic loss.






NoteA local approximation can have a different optimum



The target approaches zero in the tail, while a portfolio with \(w<1\) retains a positive cash intercept. Relative errors can therefore be large even when absolute errors are small. There is no guarantee that minimizing \(\operatorname{KL}_2\) gives a better exact-KL fit than minimizing ordinary squared error.

The gap has a trading interpretation
On the original binary tree, rebalancing to \(w=2/3\) at every binary step produces

title: Prices as information: the framework
text:
An asset distributes wealth across possible outcomes. Once we divide by its price, that distribution of wealth can also be read as a probability model. Prices, portfolios, and information then become parts of the same calculation.
Start with a simple question: if you and the market disagree about the chances of an outcome, what investment expresses your view? We will answer it with one bet, work through a football example, and see how limited trading opportunities prevent some views from being implemented exactly.
This is a web companion to Jan Vecer’s Principles of Portfolio Choice. No knowledge of information theory is needed to begin.

title: Prices as information: the framework
section: 1. Choose the unit in which we measure wealth
text:
1. Choose the unit in which we measure wealth
Fix a strictly positive traded reference asset \(Y\), held as a self-financing, total-return investment: any distributions are reinvested, rather than paid out separately. An interest-bearing account is one example. Express every price and payoff in units of \(Y\): how many units of the reference asset could you exchange it for? In these units, the reference asset itself always has value
\[
Y(t)=1.
\]
If \(Y\) is a cash account, this means measuring performance relative to that account. We write \(X(0)\) for another asset’s price now and \(X(T)\) for its value at the final date. The ratio \(X(T)/X(0)\) is its gross return in these reference units.
Begin with finitely many possible outcomes and a market that lets us buy a separate claim on each one. Each quoted state price is strictly positive; trading is frictionless and arbitrage-free. Later we will ask what changes when only a few bundled assets are available.

title: Prices as information: the framework
section: 2. Understand one claim before building a portfolio
text:
2. Understand one claim before building a portfolio
Suppose a football team can win, draw, or lose. A win claim pays one unit of \(Y\) if the team wins, and zero otherwise. Suppose it costs \(0.50\) units of \(Y\).
Spending one unit buys two such claims. If the team wins, they pay two units. Thus the claim’s price is \(q=0.5\), while its payout per unit staked—the decimal odds—is
\[
\frac{1}{q}=2.
\]
These are two descriptions of the same contract: price per claim and payout per unit spent.
Buying one claim on every outcome guarantees exactly one unit of \(Y\) at the final date. Holding one unit of the reference investment delivers the same thing. By the law of one price, the claims together cost one unit of \(Y\) now, so their prices sum to one.1 We denote this distribution of market state prices by \(\mathbb P^Y\). It is a pricing distribution; it need not agree with an investor’s assessment of the chances.

title: Prices as information: the framework
text:
3. Turn your probabilities into stakes
Suppose you have \(1{,}000\) units to invest. You assign probabilities \(0.6\), \(0.3\), and \(0.1\) to Win, Draw, and Loss. Call your belief distribution \(\mathbb P^M\).
Allocate your budget in those proportions: \(600\) to Win, \(300\) to Draw, and \(100\) to Loss. To find the number of claims bought, divide each stake by the corresponding claim price.

If Win occurs, only the win claims pay, so your final wealth is \(1{,}200\). If Draw occurs, it is \(1{,}000\); if Loss occurs, it is \(500\). The three final wealth values are alternatives, not amounts to add together.
Write \(M\) for this investment. In outcome \(\omega\), its stake is \(M(0)\mathbb P^M(\omega)\). Dividing by the price per claim gives
\[
M(T,\omega)
=\frac{M(0)\mathbb P^M(\omega)}{\mathbb P^Y(\omega)}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{M(T,\omega)}{M(0)}
=\frac{\mathbb P^M(\omega)}{\mathbb P^Y(\omega)}.
\]
This ratio of probabilities is a likelihood ratio. The win return is \(0.6/0.5=1.2\): your model puts more weight on Win than the market does, and your position pays more if Win occurs. Nothing has yet been optimized; we have simply translated probabilities into an investment.

title: Prices as information: the framework
text:
4. Run the construction backwards
A payoff can also be translated into a probability distribution. Suppose a different investment \(V\) costs \(1{,}000\) and pays \((800,1200,1200)\) in the same three outcomes. Its price is consistent with the market weights because
\[
\begin{aligned}
&0.5(800)+0.3(1200)\\
&\quad+0.2(1200)=1000.
\end{aligned}
\]
Divide its payoffs by its cost to obtain the returns \((0.8,1.2,1.2)\). Multiply those returns by the market probabilities:
\[
\mathbb P^V=(0.4,0.36,0.24).
\]
The entries sum to one. This is the distribution implied by the payoff, whether or not its owner consciously selected those probabilities. In general,
\[
\mathbb P^V(\omega)
=\frac{V(T,\omega)}{V(0)}\mathbb P^Y(\omega).
\]
The budget fixes the size of the investment; this distribution describes how its payoff is spread across outcomes. We can move in either direction: probabilities determine a payoff, and a fairly priced nonnegative payoff determines probabilities.

Even a one-dollar bet has an induced probability
Start with $100 in an idealized fair, even-money game. Bet $1 on Red and keep $99 in cash. Final wealth is $101 on Red and $99 otherwise, so the induced probabilities are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P^V
&=\left(\frac12\frac{101}{100},\frac12\frac{99}{100}\right)\\
&=(0.505,0.495).
\end{aligned}
\]
The small position is a small change from the pricing law \((0.5,0.5)\). This is a description of the portfolio, not a claim that its owner truly believes the chance of Red is \(50.5\%\).

title: Prices as information: the framework
text:
5. Measure the football investment’s performance
The football investment \(M\) has wealth multipliers \(1.2\), \(1\), and \(0.5\). A multiplier of \(1.2\) means a 20% gain; \(0.5\) means a 50% loss. Their log returns are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log(1.2)&\approx0.1823,\\
\log(1)&=0,\\
\log(0.5)&\approx-0.6931.
\end{aligned}
\]
Why logarithms? Successive wealth multipliers multiply, while their logarithms add. In repeated independent investments, average log performance approaches expected log performance, provided the log return is integrable. This makes it a measure of long-run compounded growth. We derive that connection on the relative-entropy page.
An expectation must specify which probabilities do the averaging. Start with your beliefs, \((0.6,0.3,0.1)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E^M\!\left[\log\frac{M(T)}{M(0)}\right]\\
&=0.6\log(1.2)+0.3\log(1)\\
&\quad+0.1\log(0.5)\\
&\approx0.0401.
\end{aligned}
\]
Now use the market weights, \((0.5,0.3,0.2)\), to average the same three log returns:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E^Y\!\left[\log\frac{M(T)}{M(0)}\right]\\
&=0.5\log(1.2)+0.3\log(1)\\
&\quad+0.2\log(0.5)\\
&\approx-0.0475.
\end{aligned}
\]
The market assigns twice as much weight to the loss. The investment therefore has positive expected log performance under your beliefs and negative expected log performance under the market weights. Neither average guarantees a particular outcome.

Those averages have an information interpretation
Recall that each wealth multiplier is a ratio of probabilities. For two distributions \(p\) and \(q\) on the same outcomes, define
\[
D(p\Vert q)
=\sum_i p_i\log\frac{p_i}{q_i}.
\]
For each outcome, divide its two probabilities, take the logarithm, and then average using the first distribution, \(p\). This is relative entropy, also called Kullback–Leibler divergence. Natural logarithms give units called nats.
Our first calculation is exactly this definition:
\[
D(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^Y)\approx0.0401.
\]
For the market average, reverse the order of the distributions and change the sign:
\[
-D(\mathbb P^Y\Vert\mathbb P^M)\approx-0.0475.
\]
Here “information” means average log evidence distinguishing two models. A likelihood ratio above one favors the numerator model; a ratio below one favors the denominator. Relative entropy averages that log evidence under the numerator model. It is nonnegative and vanishes only when the distributions agree. The relative-entropy page explains why and lets you examine each contribution.

text:
6. Explore the example, then generalize
Try changing the beliefs first, then the prices. Watch how stake ÷ price = final wealth in that outcome changes, along with the two expected log returns.

Every asset has the same information identity
Any fairly priced nonnegative asset \(X\) of positive cost has its own implied measure \(\mathbb P^X\), just as \(V\) does in Section 4. The same identity holds with \(X\) in place of \(M\):
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E^X\!\left[\log\frac{X(T)}{X(0)}\right]\\
=\mathbb E^X\!\left[\log\frac{d\mathbb P^X}{d\mathbb P^Y}\right]\\
=D(\mathbb P^X\Vert\mathbb P^Y).
\end{gathered}
\]
In our finite example, \(d\mathbb P^X/d\mathbb P^Y\) is simply the state-by-state probability ratio. The expectation is under \(\mathbb P^X\), the same measure as the numerator. This measure describes the asset’s payoff; it need not equal your personal belief \(\mathbb P^M\). The football investment matched those beliefs because we deliberately constructed it that way.

title: Prices as information: the framework
section: 7. What if your payoff expresses a different model?
text:
7. What if your payoff expresses a different model?
Your beliefs can stay at \(\mathbb P^M\) while you choose a payoff with implied distribution \(\mathbb P^V\). Let \(G(T)=V(T)/V(0)\) be its gross return. The expected log return now decomposes as
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E^M[\log G(T)]
&=D(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^Y)\\
&\quad-D(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^V).
\end{aligned}
\]
Read it in two steps. The first term is the information in your beliefs relative to market prices. The second is the mismatch between your beliefs and the distribution your payoff implements. Subtracting it gives your expected log performance.
Because relative entropy is nonnegative, that mismatch cannot improve expected log growth under your beliefs. Choosing \(\mathbb P^V=\mathbb P^M\) removes it. This is why the original investment \(M\) is log-optimal when all state claims are available: the optimality follows from the construction.
Now choose a payoff below. The figure calculates its implied probabilities and shows the two terms. The likelihood-ratio button returns to the payoff that expresses your beliefs exactly.




Interactive figure. It needs JavaScript.



Figure 2: Both figures share the same beliefs and prices. The information bar separates the available information from the mismatch of the chosen payoff.




The colors now have four distinct roles: market \(\mathbb P^Y\), belief \(\mathbb P^M\), asset \(\mathbb P^X\), chosen payoff \(\mathbb P^V\). Lost growth marks the mismatch penalty.







NoteSupport, zero payoffs, and attainability





Beliefs and payoffs may contain zeros. If the investor assigns positive probability to a zero-payoff state, expected log growth is \(-\infty\), and the mismatch is \(+\infty\). The finite-market identity remains valid in this extended sense.
For general scenario spaces, use densities and require \(\mathbb P^M\ll\mathbb P^Y\) and \(D(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^Y)<\infty\) for the displayed subtraction. This avoids an undefined difference of infinities.
The payoff-to-measure map requires only fair pricing and a nonnegative payoff of positive finite cost. Implementing every desired measure additionally requires a rich enough asset menu. The trinomial page shows what happens when that menu is incomplete; the portfolio laboratory finds the closest attainable distribution.

title: Prices as information: the framework
section: 8. What if only the Win contract and cash trade?
text:
8. What if only the Win contract and cash trade?
Return to the same football beliefs \((0.6,0.3,0.1)\) and prices \((0.5,0.3,0.2)\). Now remove the separate Draw and Loss claims. The Win contract costs \(0.5\) and pays \((1,0,0)\), so its return per unit invested is \(R_W=(2,0,0)\).
Invest a fraction \(w\) in that contract and the rest in the reference asset. The unit-cost portfolio pays
\[
\begin{aligned}
V_w&=1+w(R_W-1)\\
&=(1+w,1-w,1-w).
\end{aligned}
\]
It cannot distinguish Draw from Loss. Expected log growth is
\[
g(w)=0.6\log(1+w)+0.4\log(1-w).
\]
The first-order condition \(0.6/(1+w)-0.4/(1-w)=0\) gives \(w^*=0.2\). This is feasible even if borrowing and short selling are excluded. The implemented payoff is \((1.2,0.8,0.8)\) and the corresponding law is
\[
\mathbb P^{V_{0.2}}=(0.6,0.24,0.16).
\]

title: Prices as information: the framework
text:
9. Where do preferences enter?
We first translated payoffs into probabilities and established log optimality. Other preferences can now select a different payoff, and hence a different induced law \(\mathbb P^U\). A positive payoff selected by utility is itself log-optimal under \(\mathbb P^U\). The original belief remains \(\mathbb P^M\); these two laws need not agree.
For example, CRRA utility with relative risk aversion \(\gamma\) selects the normalized payoff
\[
\begin{gathered}
G^U=\frac{L_M^{1/\gamma}}{\mathbb E^Y[L_M^{1/\gamma}]},\\
L_M=\frac{d\mathbb P^M}{d\mathbb P^Y},
\end{gathered}
\]
when all state claims are available. At \(\gamma=1\), the denominator is one and \(\mathbb P^U=\mathbb P^M\). The utility page explains the change of law, compares it with keeping a cash reserve, and distinguishes a full-menu target from constrained utility optimization.

title: Prices as information: the framework
text:
From probabilities to price processes
The same language extends through time: a positive traded asset’s relative price is a likelihood-ratio process on the information observed so far. The dynamics page connects this construction with classical martingale pricing.
Linear information flow is one useful modeling class. Its binomial, negative-binomial, normal, Poisson, gamma, and inverse-Gaussian examples share an additive information clock. They are supporting model families: the payoff, information, and portfolio principles above do not depend on choosing one of them. Begin with the binary example to connect likelihoods with the familiar stock-and-cash replication formula.

title: Prices as information: the framework
text:
Continue by financial question
The portfolio-choice overview brings the next steps together.

Discrete hedging: rebalance a normal-model option hedge and compare the resulting payoffs and densities.







NoteA further connection: statistical testing





The market measure \(\mathbb P^Y\) can serve as a null model, and an asset or portfolio measure as an alternative. A fairly priced, normalized, nonnegative payoff is an e-value: its expectation under the null is one. Consistent likelihood ratios through time form a nonnegative martingale. Ville’s inequality then controls the chance, under the null, of ever crossing a chosen evidence threshold. Explore it in the binomial model.



Kelly (1956) connected information rate and capital growth; Cover and Thomas give the finite horse-race identity. Geman, El Karoui, and Rochet developed the change-of-numeraire relation between traded assets and probability measures. This site uses these connections as a common language for pricing and portfolio choice.
The book continues with hedging as density approximation in Chapter 6 and learning and Bayesian portfolios in Chapter 7. The Bayesian learning page explains when wealth shares follow Bayes, how partial commitment changes the update, and why adapting to a new regime requires more than reducing exposure. The presentations and resources give complementary routes through these ideas.

title: Linear information flows
text:
This chapter develops six families of price dynamics: binomial, negative binomial, normal, Poisson, gamma, and inverse Gaussian. Each model has its own section in the navigation. They share a structure: an observable driver \(Z(t)\) accumulates information, two measures give different probabilities to its increments, and price is the likelihood ratio of those two models.
The driver is additive; the price is multiplicative. “Linear information flow” refers to the affine log likelihood and its expected accumulation, not to a price moving along a straight line.

title: Linear information flows
text:
Add increments, multiply likelihoods
Suppose nonoverlapping increments are independent under each of two consistent process laws. Their densities or mass functions belong to the same time-scaled exponential family:
\[
f(z,t;\theta)=h(z,t)\exp\{\theta z-t\kappa(\theta)\}.
\]
Keep the common base \(h(z,t)\) and any shared shape or variance parameters fixed. Change the natural parameter from \(\theta_Y\) to \(\theta_X\). The base cancels:
\[
\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}=aZ(t)+bt,
\]
where the two constants are
\[
a=\theta_X-\theta_Y,
\]
\[
b=-\{\kappa(\theta_X)-\kappa(\theta_Y)\}.
\]
The likelihood ratio of a full sequence of increments has exactly the same form, because their sums are \(Z(t)\) and \(t\). Thus the terminal statistic retains the information needed to compare this particular pair of process models. Independently chosen densities at unrelated horizons would not guarantee such a consistent process.

title: Linear information flows
section: Why the expected information is linear
text:
Why the expected information is linear
If \(\mathbb E^X[Z(t)]=m_Xt\), then the two laws of observations through time \(t\) satisfy
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(\mathbb P^X\Vert\mathbb P^Y)
&=\mathbb E^X\!\left[\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}\right]\\
&=k_Xt,
\end{aligned}
\]
with \(k_X=am_X+b\geq0\). Under the market measure the expected log price goes the other way:
\[
\mathbb E^Y\!\left[\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}\right]
=-k_Yt,
\]
where \(k_Y\) is the reverse divergence over one unit of time. The two information rates need not be equal. Their signs describe the same position evaluated by two different models.
Prices still satisfy \(\mathbb E^Y[X(t)]=X(0)\). There is no contradiction: the logarithm is concave, so mean wealth and mean log wealth are different quantities.

title: Linear information flows
text:
