Binomial time is an integer trial count. In our negative-binomial example, time counts completed shocks: down moves followed by one up move. Each shock contains a random number of binary trials. The two discrete pages use the same pricing, stock, and investor laws, so the clock change can be followed numerically. Normal, Poisson, gamma, and inverse Gaussian processes can be observed on any positive time grid. Their increment distributions remain in the same family with the appropriate time scaling.
The investor’s law \(\mathbb P^M\) can be another member of the same family. Then \(D(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^Y)\) measures ideal log growth; \(D(\mathbb P^X\Vert\mathbb P^Y)\) is the stock’s expected log return under its own induced law. They coincide only if those laws coincide. Whether the investor’s ideal payoff can be implemented depends on the available securities and trading times, as the discrete comparison shows.

title: Linear information flows
text:
A common scale for comparison
A raw parameter change has different meanings across families. Moving a Poisson intensity by one is not comparable to moving a normal mean by one. The forward KL rate \(k_X\) gives a common information scale: nats per unit of the stated clock.
The continuous-model laboratories therefore start from a chosen \(k_X\), then infer the compatible second parameter. Additional controls change the event rate or shape of the information stream. Two models can have the same information rate and still produce very different paths, downside behavior, and higher moments.
These bounded controls are teaching choices. They are not fitted market parameters or limits imposed by the theory. In particular, fixing forward KL does not fix reverse KL or every tail risk.

title: Linear information flows
text:
What a simulated path shows

Normal: exact Gaussian increments on the chosen grid; joining them visually does not resolve the Brownian motion between grid points.
Poisson: finite event activity; arrivals produce visible price jumps, with deterministic movement between them.
Gamma and inverse Gaussian: infinitely many small jumps in every positive interval. Exact increment sampling gives exact distributions at the grid times; the display does not locate all intervening jumps.

The asset price may have upward or downward jumps depending on the sign of \(a\), even when the information driver only increases. For all families, the likelihood ratio is evaluated without discretizing an SDE. Exact finite-increment simulation is also available in classical models when their transition law is known—the normal/GBM example is a direct instance of that agreement.

title: Linear information flows
text:
Where to go next
Use normal and GBM for the connection with stochastic calculus, Poisson for a visible jump clock, then gamma and inverse Gaussian for infinite activity. The negative-binomial model provides the cleanest comparison of different sampling clocks carrying the same likelihood evidence.
Source: Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice, Chapter 5, “Dynamic Price Models with Linear Information Flow.”

title: Mean–variance & information
text:
Mean–variance analysis describes a portfolio through its expected return and a quadratic measure of risk. The information-theoretic perspective describes its whole payoff through an induced distribution. The connection becomes precise once we specify which measure supplies the quadratic penalty, and where the approximation is taken.
Use \(G=V(T)/V(0)\) for a gross payoff and \(Z=G-1\) for its excess return, all in units of \(Y\). Fair pricing means \(\mathbb E^Y[G]=1\), hence \(\mathbb E^Y[Z]=0\).

title: Mean–variance & information
text:
Start with classical mean–variance
Let \(r\) be the vector of asset excess returns. With a reference asset available, risky weights \(w\) produce \(Z=w^\top r\); the remaining budget goes into the reference asset. Define
\[
\mu=\mathbb E^M[r],
\]
\[
\Sigma_M=\operatorname{Cov}^M(r).
\]
Classical mean–variance with risk penalty \(\lambda>0\) maximizes
\[
w^\top\mu-\frac\lambda2w^\top\Sigma_Mw.
\]
Both the mean and covariance are evaluated under the investor’s probability model. When \(\Sigma_M\) is positive definite and there are no constraints on risky positions,
\[
w^*=\frac1\lambda\Sigma_M^{-1}\mu.
\]
This formula does not check that terminal wealth stays nonnegative. Budget, leverage, short-sale and solvency constraints must be imposed separately. Under constraints, the solution is a quadratic program rather than this inverse-matrix formula.

title: Mean–variance & information
text:
The ordinary Taylor approximation
For \(Z\) near zero,
\[
\log(1+Z)=Z-\frac12Z^2+O(Z^3).
\]
Taking expectation under the investor’s belief gives
\[
T_M(Z)=\mathbb E^M[Z]-\frac12\mathbb E^M[Z^2].
\]
The penalty is a second moment, not just a variance:
\[
\mathbb E^M[Z^2]
=\operatorname{Var}^M(Z)+(\mathbb E^M[Z])^2.
\]
Thus the literal second-order approximation to expected log growth differs from classical mean–variance with \(\lambda=1\). It becomes unreliable near \(Z=-1\), where log utility diverges but the quadratic remains finite.

title: Mean–variance & information
text:
The book’s mixed-measure quadratic
The likelihood construction leads to another objective,
\[
J(Z)=\mathbb E^M[Z]-\frac12\mathbb E^Y[Z^2].
\]
Beliefs determine the expected reward; prices determine the quadratic geometry. Because \(\mathbb E^Y[Z]=0\), the penalty here also equals \(\tfrac12\operatorname{Var}^Y(Z)\).
This objective has an exact information interpretation. Set
\[
L_M=\frac{d\mathbb P^M}{d\mathbb P^Y},
\qquad
\chi^2=\mathbb E^Y[(L_M-1)^2].
\]
Completing the square gives
\[
J(Z)=\frac12\chi^2
-\frac12\mathbb E^Y[(G-L_M)^2].
\]
Write \(Q(G)=\mathbb E^Y[(G-L_M)^2]\) for the ordinary squared-error loss, without a factor of \(1/2\). Then \(J=\chi^2/2-Q(G)/2\): maximizing \(J\) is exactly equivalent to minimizing \(Q\). The factor of \(1/2\) belongs to the reward objective \(J\), while the loss \(Q\) uses the same convention as the comparison page.
The first term is fixed. Maximizing \(J\) chooses the attainable payoff closest to the likelihood ratio \(L_M\) in squared error under the pricing measure. In a complete market, \(G=L_M\) is attainable and achieves the maximum \(\chi^2/2\) exactly. We reserve \(R\) for a traded asset’s gross return.






NoteExact optimizer does not mean exact growth value



In a complete market, both log growth and this mixed quadratic select \(G=L_M\). Their objective values are different: the log optimum is \(D(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^Y)\), whereas the quadratic optimum is \(\chi^2/2\). In a restricted asset menu, their best attainable portfolios can also differ.








NoteThe square-completion argument





Since \(\mathbb E^Y[Z]=0\),
\[
\mathbb E^M[Z]=\mathbb E^Y[(L_M-1)Z].
\]
For real numbers \(a,z\), the identity \(az-z^2/2=a^2/2-(z-a)^2/2\) applies state by state with \(a=L_M-1\). Taking \(\mathbb E^Y\) proves the formula. The continuous-state version requires \(L_M-1\) and \(Z\) to be square integrable.

title: Mean–variance & information
section: A different expansion: close to the desired payoff
text:
A different expansion: close to the desired payoff
The near-cash Taylor expansion uses \(G\approx1\). A target-centered expansion instead uses \(G\approx L_M\). For a strictly positive target \(L_M\) and an equal-cost positive approximation \(G\), define
\[
\delta=\frac{G-L_M}{L_M}.
\]
Because both payoffs cost one, \(\mathbb E^M[\delta]=\mathbb E^Y[G-L_M]=0\). Expanding \(-\log(1+\delta)\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^G)
&=-\mathbb E^M[\log(1+\delta)]\\
&\approx\frac12\mathbb E^M[\delta^2]\\
&=\frac12\mathbb E^Y\left[\frac{(G-L_M)^2}{L_M}\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
This criterion is \(\operatorname{KL}_2=\tfrac12\chi^2(\mathbb P^G\Vert\mathbb P^M)\). Its weight \(1/L_M\) emphasizes errors relative to the target size. It differs from ordinary quadratic hedging, which minimizes \(\mathbb E^Y[(G-L_M)^2]\).
For \(G=1+w(R-1)\), its unconstrained regression coefficient is
\[
w_{\mathrm{KL}_2}
=\frac{\mathbb E^Y[(R-1)(L_M-1)/L_M]}
{\mathbb E^Y[(R-1)^2/L_M]},
\]
provided these moments are finite and the denominator is positive. Feasibility still needs to be checked.






NoteTwo different notions of ‘small’



Small absolute payoff error is not enough for the target-centered expansion when \(L_M\) can approach zero. A sufficient condition is uniformly small relative error, with integrability controlling the Taylor remainder. In the geometric-shock example, KL2 selects \(w=0.8125\), ordinary quadratic hedging selects \(0.7\), and exact KL selects approximately \(0.745331\). The local approximation does not rank those portfolios by exact growth.


Ordinary quadratic hedging emerges in an additional near-cash limit. If \(L_M=1+\varepsilon h\) and \(G=1+\varepsilon a\), with bounded \(h,a\) of zero \(\mathbb P^Y\) mean, then
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^G)
=\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}\mathbb E^Y[(h-a)^2]+O(\varepsilon^3).
\]
Here both beliefs relative to prices and the chosen payoff approach the reference asset. A target far from cash need not have this unweighted local geometry.

title: Mean–variance & information
text:
Experiment with the approximation
The tool uses three scenarios and a portfolio of the reference asset and one risky asset. Its illustrative inputs are \(q=(0.30,0.40,0.30)\) and \(\mathbb P^X=(0.60,0.30,0.10)\). Belief strength moves the investor from \(q\) toward \((0.50,0.35,0.15)\). These are an asymmetric teaching example, chosen so the optimizers can differ.
Change belief strength, move the risky allocation \(w\) between zero and one, and compare exact growth with the ordinary Taylor and mixed quadratic objectives. Use each optimizer to see whether it chooses the same position.




Interactive comparison. It needs JavaScript.



Figure 1: The exact log criterion and two quadratic criteria share a zero value at the reference asset. Their differences grow as the payoff moves away from one. The tool uses the stated finite scenario model and the displayed allocation bounds.



The approximation depends on the size of statewise returns, not just on an apparently small average return. A small mean can coexist with a substantial probability of a nearly zero payoff.






NoteWhen do the two quadratic penalties agree locally?





Their difference is
\[
T_M(Z)-J(Z)
=-\frac12\mathbb E^Y[(L_M-1)Z^2].
\]
If both \(L_M-1\) and \(Z\) are uniformly of order \(\varepsilon\), this difference is of order \(\varepsilon^3\). In the same regime, both approximate expected log growth to second order. Small returns alone justify the ordinary Taylor expansion; using the pricing measure in the quadratic penalty also needs control of the difference between beliefs and prices, or the separate Pearson projection interpretation.

title: Mean–variance & information
section: From payoffs to a portfolio calculation
text:
From payoffs to a portfolio calculation
For excess-return vector \(r\) with \(\mathbb E^Y[r]=0\), define
\[
\Sigma_Y=\mathbb E^Y[rr^\top].
\]
The mixed objective becomes
\[
J(w)=w^\top\mu-\frac12w^\top\Sigma_Yw.
\]
With invertible \(\Sigma_Y\) and unconstrained risky weights, its solution is
\[
w^*=\Sigma_Y^{-1}\mu.
\]
The matrix resembles the classical covariance formula, but its entries come from \(\mathbb P^Y\). A singular matrix can reflect redundant assets; removing redundancy or solving the constrained program avoids treating its inverse as defined. Even when the matrix is invertible, an unrestricted projection can produce negative wealth. The portfolio laboratory keeps long-only cost weights and nonnegative payoffs.

title: Mean–variance & information
section: Three geometries for a restricted menu
text:
Three geometries for a restricted menu
In finite states, write \(p_i=\mathbb P^M(i)\), \(q_i=\mathbb P^Y(i)\) and \(v_i=\mathbb P^V(i)\). Then \(G(i)=v_i/q_i\), and the projection problems are:







Objective
Mismatch minimized




Exact expected log growth
\(D(p\Vert v)\)


Target-centered KL2
\(\tfrac12\sum_i(v_i-p_i)^2/p_i\)


Mixed quadratic / ordinary quadratic hedge
\(Q(G)=\sum_i(v_i-p_i)^2/q_i\)



KL2 is half the Pearson divergence \(\chi^2(v\Vert p)\); its factor of \(1/2\) comes from the Taylor expansion of KL. The ordinary quadratic loss \(Q\) uses the fixed market distribution in its denominator and has no factor of \(1/2\). Multiplying either loss by a positive constant leaves its minimizing portfolio unchanged. Neither expression is \(\chi^2(p\Vert v)\), whose denominator would be \(v_i\).
If the investor’s distribution is attainable, all three mismatches can reach zero. Otherwise the geometry matters: the nearest feasible distribution in KL divergence need not be the nearest under either squared distance. The worked comparison calculates all three and lets you vary the pricing law.
Continue: enter several asset densities and compare the resulting allocations in the portfolio laboratory.






NoteBook connection





Based on Chapter 3 of Jan Vecer’s Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective: “Mean-Variance Portfolio Optimization,” “Mean–variance as a quadratic approximation to log growth,” and the Pearson duality and projection results. The separate treatment of classical covariance, ordinary Taylor second moments and the mixed quadratic follows the distinctions made in that chapter.

title: Normal → geometric Brownian motion
text:
The binomial model turns two probabilities into two price multipliers. The normal model does the same with two densities. Start with two normal laws for one observation; their ratio produces geometric Brownian motion exactly.
Throughout, \(X(t)\) is measured in units of the reference asset \(Y\). The pricing measure is \(\mathbb P^Y\); the asset-induced measure is \(\mathbb P^X\). An investor’s belief \(\mathbb P^M\) remains a separate choice.

title: Normal → geometric Brownian motion
text:
One driver, two normal laws
Let \(R(t)\) have independent increments and a common variance rate \(s^2>0\), but different mean rates:
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(t)&\sim N(\mu_Yt,s^2t)
&&\text{under }\mathbb P^Y,\\
R(t)&\sim N(\mu_Xt,s^2t)
&&\text{under }\mathbb P^X.
\end{aligned}
\]
At each horizon \(t>0\), write the two densities with the same formula, for \(j\in\{X,Y\}\):
\[
f_j(z,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi s^2t}}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{(z-\mu_jt)^2}{2s^2t}\right].
\]
The normalizing constants cancel in their ratio. Expanding the two squares leaves a straight line in \(z\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log\frac{f_X(z,t)}{f_Y(z,t)}
&=-\frac{(z-\mu_Xt)^2}{2s^2t}\\
&\quad+\frac{(z-\mu_Yt)^2}{2s^2t}\\
&=az+bt,
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
a=\frac{\mu_X-\mu_Y}{s^2},
\qquad
b=-\frac{\mu_X^2-\mu_Y^2}{2s^2}.
\]
Consequently, the price is already determined:
\[
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}=\exp\{aR(t)+bt\}.
\]
This is linear information flow: log price is affine in the observed statistic and time. Linear information flow does not mean that price or the driver follows a straight path.

title: Normal → geometric Brownian motion
text:
Explore the model
The figure fixes \(s=1\) and \(\mu_Y=0\). Choose the information rate \(k\); the other mean follows as \(\mu_X=\sqrt{2k}\). The densities, price response and paths all use the same parameters.

The interactive model requires JavaScript. With \(k=0.05\), the driver mean rates are \(0\) and \(\sqrt{0.1}\), the price volatility is \(\sqrt{0.1}\), and the expected log-price rates are \(+0.05\) under \(\mathbb P^X\) and \(-0.05\) under \(\mathbb P^Y\).

title: Normal → geometric Brownian motion
text:
Recover the classical GBM solution
Under the pricing measure, write \(R(t)=\mu_Yt+sW^Y(t)\) and define the signed price loading
\[
\eta=\frac{\mu_X-\mu_Y}{s}.
\]
Substitution into the likelihood ratio gives
\[
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}
=\exp\!\left\{\eta W^Y(t)-\frac12\eta^2t\right\}.
\]
This is exactly the solution of the discounted geometric Brownian motion equation
\[
\frac{dX(t)}{X(t)}=\eta\,dW^Y(t).
\]
Under the asset measure, \(R(t)=\mu_Xt+sW^X(t)\) instead, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}
&=\exp\!\left\{\eta W^X(t)+\frac12\eta^2t\right\},\\
\frac{dX(t)}{X(t)}
&=\eta^2dt+\eta\,dW^X(t).
\end{aligned}
\]
The price volatility is \(|\eta|\), not generally the driver scale \(s\). The information rate is \(k=\eta^2/2\), with units of nats per time unit. Volatility and information rate therefore have different units. The book’s convenient normalization \(\mu_Y=0\), \(\mu_X=s^2\) makes \(a=1\) and \(|\eta|=s\); that equality follows from the normalization.

title: Normal → geometric Brownian motion
section: The same model, read in the other direction
text:
The same model, read in the other direction







Dynamics first
Likelihood first




Specify the pricing-measure GBM equation.
Specify two normal laws with a common variance.


Solve for the exponential price.
Divide the two densities.


Recover the asset measure by the price tilt.
Read off the GBM equation if desired.



The two routes give the same process. A differential equation makes local evolution explicit. The likelihood formulation makes the pair of measures and the finite-horizon price formula explicit.

title: Normal → geometric Brownian motion
section: Information is the drift of log price
text:
Information is the drift of log price
The two divergences are equal in this same-variance normal family. In the formulas below, the measures describe observations through the chosen horizon \(t\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(\mathbb P^X\Vert\mathbb P^Y)&=kt,\\
D(\mathbb P^Y\Vert\mathbb P^X)&=kt,\\
k&=\frac{(\mu_X-\mu_Y)^2}{2s^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Accordingly, expected log price is \(+kt\) under \(\mathbb P^X\) and \(-kt\) under \(\mathbb P^Y\). Meanwhile the expected price under \(\mathbb P^Y\) remains \(X(0)\). A mean-zero price return and a negative expected log return are compatible.
The model is consistent at every time scale: increments over a period \(\Delta t\) are normal with mean \(\mu_j\Delta t\) and variance \(s^2\Delta t\). Refining the observation grid changes the view of a path, not the model’s horizon law.
The same two normal laws also give Black–Scholes prices and option densities. For a portfolio held between trading dates, discrete hedging compares its density with the target claim’s density.
Continue: replace continuous fluctuations with counted events in the Poisson model, or return to the shared construction in linear information flow.






NoteSource and conventions





Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, Chapter 5, “Normal family (Brownian driver).” This page uses \(s\) for driver scale and \(\eta\) for price loading to keep their roles distinct. All prices are denominated in \(Y\).

title: Poisson: events become price jumps
text: In the normal model, the observation is a continuous return driver. Here it is an event count. The pricing measure and the asset measure attach different probabilities to the same sequence of arrivals; their likelihood ratio determines how the price responds to each arrival.

title: Poisson: events become price jumps
text:
Two arrival rates
Let \(N(t)\) count events. Under measure \(\mathbb P^j\), for \(j\in\{X,Y\}\), use a Poisson process with intensity \(\lambda_j>0\):
\[
N(t)\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_jt).
\]
The mass assigned to \(n\) events is
\[
f_j(n,t)=e^{-\lambda_jt}\frac{(\lambda_jt)^n}{n!}.
\]
The factorial and the common power of \(t\) cancel when the two masses are divided:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}
&=\left(\frac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y}\right)^{N(t)}
e^{(\lambda_Y-\lambda_X)t},\\
\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}&=aN(t)+bt,
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
a=\log\frac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y},
\qquad b=\lambda_Y-\lambda_X.
\]
This is again linear information flow. The count is sufficient for the likelihood ratio: with constant intensities, the precise arrival times carry no further likelihood information once the horizon and total count are known.

title: Poisson: events become price jumps
section: Explore arrival frequency and price response
text:
Explore arrival frequency and price response
Choose a pricing intensity, an information rate and a jump direction. The figure solves for \(\lambda_X\) from those choices. The intensity ratio, and hence the size of a price jump, is derived rather than chosen independently.

The interactive model requires JavaScript. Its default pricing intensity is \(\lambda_Y=3\) and the information rate is \(k=0.05\) nats per time unit; the asset intensity is chosen on the downward-jump branch.

title: Poisson: events become price jumps
section: Read the path from the two rates
text:
Read the path from the two rates
At an arrival, \(N\) increases by one and the price is multiplied by
\[
\frac{X(t)}{X(t-)}=\frac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y}.
\]
Between arrivals, log price changes at the deterministic rate \(b=\lambda_Y-\lambda_X\).



Rate comparison
At an event
Between events




\(\lambda_X>\lambda_Y\)
Price jumps up.
Price drifts down.


\(\lambda_X<\lambda_Y\)
Price jumps down.
Price drifts up.


\(\lambda_X=\lambda_Y\)
No price response.
Price is constant.



An event that the asset measure regards as more likely than the pricing measure favors the asset measure, so its likelihood-ratio price rises. The drift compensates for this jump response and preserves the pricing-measure martingale identity.
If a local dynamics description is useful, the same process satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dX(t)}{X(t-)}
&=(r-1)\{dN(t)-\lambda_Ydt\},\\
r&=\frac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Under \(\mathbb P^Y\), the expression in braces is a compensated Poisson increment. This equation is a consequence of the likelihood specification.

title: Poisson: events become price jumps
section: The two information rates need not match

title: Poisson: events become price jumps
text:
Exact at every horizon
Independent counts add: Poisson laws with means \(\lambda_js\) and \(\lambda_jt\) sum to a Poisson law with mean \(\lambda_j(s+t)\). The same model therefore works at daily, hourly or finer horizons. In the figure, exponential waiting times produce actual arrival times and the finite sequence of jumps, with the exact drift between them.
Continue: the gamma model replaces a count of isolated events with accumulated positive activity, generated by infinitely many small jumps.






NoteSource and conventions





Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, Chapter 5, “Poisson family (counting driver).” The price is measured in units of \(Y\). The asset measure \(\mathbb P^X\) is a subjective investor model only when the investor chooses \(\mathbb P^M=\mathbb P^X\).

title: Pricing and hedging
text:
A hedge starts with a target claim and the assets available to reproduce it. Information theory supplies a probability representation of both the target and the implemented position.
Fix a pricing law \(\mathbb P^Y\) and a nonnegative claim \(H\) with finite, positive price \(H(0)=\mathbb E^Y[H]\). Its induced law is
\[
\mathbb P^H(\omega)
=\mathbb P^Y(\omega)\frac{H(\omega)}{H(0)}.
\]
The formula is written for finite or countable outcomes; densities give the corresponding continuous-state construction. A claim that vanishes on some outcomes induces a law with zero mass there. All payoffs and prices here use the reference asset as numeraire.

title: Pricing and hedging
text:
Exact replication matches the distribution
In two states, cash and a nonconstant stock span every payoff. The usual delta hedge and the mixture of induced probability laws express the same replication. The binomial tutorial connects shares, cost weights, and probability matching in one numerical example.

title: Pricing and hedging
section: Incomplete trading leaves a choice of criterion
text:
Incomplete trading leaves a choice of criterion
With more outcomes than independent traded payoffs, exact replication may fail. Squared payoff error, target-relative quadratic error, and exact relative entropy can then choose different hedges.
The three-criteria comparison uses a single negative-binomial market throughout. It explains the weighting and loss function of each criterion, compares the optimal portfolios, and identifies which conclusions survive a change of pricing law.
The information interpretation must retain the target measure. Minimizing \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^H\Vert\mathbb P^V)\) maximizes expected log payoff under the claim-induced law \(\mathbb P^H\) for equal-cost positive candidates. This criterion is distinct from minimizing payoff error under a pricing or physical law.

title: Pricing and hedging
text:
Options are distributions too
The options page displays the probability law induced by a call, put, digital, or straddle. It connects familiar option-price formulas with weighted tail probabilities and shows how a cash reserve changes the induced distribution.

title: Pricing and hedging
text:
Rebalance over a finite interval
The discrete hedging laboratory projects a target onto stock and cash over one conditional trading interval in a normal model. It separates approximation error from positivity constraints and explains when the short-interval hedge approaches the classical delta.
For the portfolio-selection interpretation of the same geometry, continue with beliefs and attainable portfolios.

title: The trinomial model
text:
The binomial model has just enough traded payoffs to distinguish its two states. A third state exposes two separate issues: which pricing measure fits the traded returns, and which investor beliefs can be implemented by trading?
Work in units of \(Y\) and take the book’s three-state stock return:
\[
R^X=\left(\frac32,1,\frac12\right).
\]
Only \(X\) and \(Y\) are traded. Every state is possible; borrowing and short selling are available unless a portfolio constraint is explicitly imposed.

title: The trinomial model
section: First, find all consistent pricing measures
text:
First, find all consistent pricing measures
The pricing weights must satisfy
\[
q_1+q_2+q_3=1,
\]
\[
\frac32q_1+q_2+\frac12q_3=1.
\]
Subtracting these equations gives \(q_1=q_3\). Thus the positive pricing measures form a line:
\[
\mathbb P^Y(t)=(t,1-2t,t),
\qquad 0<t<\frac12.
\]
Each choice gives an asset measure by multiplying the pricing weights by the stock return:
\[
\mathbb P^X(t)
=\left(\frac{3t}{2},1-2t,\frac t2\right).
\]
Both martingale checks now hold:
\[
\mathbb E^Y[R^X]=1,
\qquad
\mathbb E^X[1/R^X]=1.
\]
The first prices \(X\) in units of \(Y\). The second prices \(Y\) in units of \(X\). Choosing another \(t\) changes both measures while preserving the same stock returns.

title: The trinomial model
text:
Then choose an attainable portfolio
Put a fraction \(w\) of initial wealth in \(X\), and \(1-w\) in \(Y\). Its return is
\[
R^{V,w}
=\left(1+\frac w2,1,1-\frac w2\right).
\]
For a fixed pricing measure, its implied density is
\[
\mathbb P^{V,w}
=(1-w)\mathbb P^Y+w\mathbb P^X.
\]
With no short sales, \(0\le w\le1\): the investor can move along a line segment in the probability triangle. Allowing borrowing and short selling extends the line; nonnegative terminal wealth imposes \(-2\le w\le2\). Neither case fills the triangle.

The interactive figure requires JavaScript. At the book’s default \(t=1/3\), the pricing measure is \((1/3,1/3,1/3)\) and the stock measure is \((1/2,1/3,1/6)\). Every stock-and-cash portfolio retains middle-state probability \(1/3\).

The left triangle varies the pricing rule, holding the stock’s returns fixed. The right triangle varies the portfolio, holding the selected pricing rule fixed. Each corner represents all probability concentrated on one state; interior points assign weight to all three.

title: The trinomial model
section: Why a belief can be unattainable
text:
Why a belief can be unattainable
At the book’s choice \(t=1/3\),
\[
\mathbb P^{V,w}
=\left(\frac{2+w}{6},\frac13,\frac{2-w}{6}\right).
\]
Now consider the investor’s beliefs
\[
\mathbb P^M=\left(\frac12,\frac16,\frac13\right).
\]
Every attainable portfolio has middle-state weight \(1/3\), while the investor assigns \(1/6\). No choice of \(w\) can make the two distributions equal. The unrestricted likelihood payoff \(\mathbb P^M/\mathbb P^Y\) exists as a mathematical claim, but it cannot be replicated using only this stock and cash.
The best attainable portfolio instead minimizes
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^{V,w}).
\]
Equivalently, it maximizes
\[
\begin{aligned}
g(w)&=\frac12\log\left(1+\frac w2\right)\\
&\quad+\frac13\log\left(1-\frac w2\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the maximizing weight is \(w=2/5\), under either of the displayed constraints. The figure shows its remaining information mismatch. This weight depends on the beliefs and the traded returns, so it stays the same as \(t\) changes. The two divergences in the growth decomposition change together.






NoteA useful special case



At \(t=5/12\), this particular belief lies on the attainable line and the mismatch vanishes at \(w=2/5\). The market remains incomplete: implementing one selected belief does not mean that every payoff is spanned.

title: The trinomial model
section: The exact decision is pricing-law invariant
text:
The exact decision is pricing-law invariant
For any strictly positive pricing law \(q(t)\) consistent with the stock and cash, and any positive unit-cost portfolio \(V_w\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^M\Vert q(t)V_w)\\
&\quad=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^M\Vert q(t))
-\mathbb E^M[\log V_w].
\end{aligned}
\]
Hold beliefs, traded returns, and the feasible portfolio set fixed. The first term depends on the pricing-law choice, but not on \(w\). Thus exact KL selects the same portfolio under every \(t\). Quadratic hedging of the corresponding ideal target \(L_M=\mathbb P^M/q(t)\) instead gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
w_Q(t)&=\frac{\mathbb E^M[R^X]-1}{\operatorname{Var}^{q(t)}(R^X)}\\

title: The trinomial model
section: The closest pricing law describes attainable growth
text:
The closest pricing law describes attainable growth
There is also a dual question: among all laws that price the traded assets, which is closest to the investor’s beliefs? In this finite-state example, the exact optimum is interior, all belief probabilities are positive, and wealth is strictly positive. Write
\[
\begin{aligned}
V^*&=(6/5,1,4/5),\\
Q^*_i&=\frac{\mathbb P^M_i}{V^*_i}
=\left(\frac5{12},\frac16,\frac5{12}\right)_i.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is precisely the pricing law \(t=5/12\) identified above. The first-order condition gives
\[
\mathbb E^M\left[\frac{R^X-1}{V^*}\right]=0.
\]
Using \(V^*=1+w^*(R^X-1)\) then gives \(\mathbb E^M[1/V^*]=1\). Therefore \(Q^*\) sums to one and \(\mathbb E^{Q^*}[R^X]=1\): it really is a pricing law.
For every other positive pricing law \(Q\) and every positive attainable unit-cost portfolio \(V\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^M\Vert Q)\\
&\quad=\mathbb E^M[\log V]
+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^M\Vert QV)\\
&\quad\geq\mathbb E^M[\log V].
\end{aligned}
\]
At \(Q^*,V^*\), the last divergence vanishes. Hence
\[
\max_V\mathbb E^M[\log V]
=\min_{Q\text{ pricing law}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^M\Vert Q).
\]






NoteScope of the reciprocal construction



The proof uses an interior optimum with all traded risky directions locally available in both signs. A binding portfolio constraint generally replaces the first-order equality by inequalities. In that case \(\mathbb P^M/V^*\) should not automatically be called a probability or an equivalent pricing law; the appropriate dual object must respect the constraints. Infinite-state extensions additionally need integrability and existence conditions. The finite example above meets the stated requirements.

title: The trinomial model
section: Incompleteness also leaves a price range
text:
Incompleteness also leaves a price range
A claim paying one in the middle state and zero otherwise would have price
\[
C(0)=\mathbb P^Y(\omega_2)=1-2t.
\]
The original stock and cash prices permit every value in \((0,1)\). This is an open no-arbitrage interval; its endpoints are limiting bounds, not admissible prices when all three states remain possible. Trading that additional claim at a price inside the interval would identify \(t\) and complete this one-period market.
This is the distinction behind the fundamental theorem of asset pricing: no arbitrage gives existence of a pricing measure; completeness gives uniqueness. A likelihood description respects the same distinction.

title: Relative-entropy tests of market efficiency
text:
What the paper asks
How can we express departures from a market-efficiency benchmark in units of information, test them statistically, and distinguish that information from what a specified trading strategy can attain?
The paper studies symbolic and finite-alphabet representations of market data. It connects conditional relative entropy, likelihood-ratio inference, and expected logarithmic growth while keeping the information set and available trading opportunities explicit.

title: Relative-entropy tests of market efficiency
text:
Main connections

A statistical benchmark: conditional relative entropy measures departure from the chosen reference law. Finite-alphabet likelihood-ratio statistics give this population quantity a statistical counterpart.
The effect of coarsening: a simpler observation alphabet can discard population information. Its effect on statistical power also depends on the test and sampling problem.
Attainable growth: information and trading gains agree under the appropriate payoff and trading assumptions. A restricted strategy set can implement only part of the available information.

title: Relative-entropy tests of market efficiency
text:
Empirical illustration
A daily S&P 500 illustration uses a bounded cash/index allocation. It finds no statistically significant improvement for that tested allocation. The framework therefore separates an information measure, evidence against a benchmark, and a demonstrated trading advantage.
